fact: Syphilis remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide.
The bacterium causing syphilis, Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum, has evolved into a highly distinctive organism that is only able to survive and be propagated in mammals.
Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum can evade the human immune system for decades with devastating consequences.
Only a minority of the predicted proteins of Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum have been detected experimentally thus far.

Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum cannot be cultured in vitro, so the researchers cultured Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum in rabbits and analyzed extracted proteins using different mass spectrometry methods.
In this study, the researchers detected more than half of the predicted number of proteins that could be expressed by Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum, totaling 557 proteins.
For approximately half of the detected proteins, the researchers succeeded in characterizing their predicted cellular location using an array of bioinformatic tools and catalogued their function.
This study provides the most comprehensive analysis of the Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum proteome to date.
Consistently wearing shoes may help in preventing onset or progression of a wide range of Neglected Tropical Diseases (NTDs).
This study assessed the factors that influenced shoe wearing behaviors among people living in a rural community in highland Ethiopia.
In the rural community in highland Ethiopia, a substantial proportion of people are at risk for podoconiosis, a debilitating lower leg condition that can be prevented by wearing shoes.
The researchers conducted semi-structured individual interviews, focus group discussions, and extended case studies among 242 adults and systematically analyzed the information.
Shoe wearing is intermittent in the rural community in highland Ethiopia.
Different factors such as cost and ability to use the shoes for certain activities, such as farming, influenced consistent shoe wearing for most people in the rural community in highland Ethiopia.
Some factors such as shoe size and fear of stigma were more relevant for podoconiosis patients in the rural community in highland Ethiopia.
Social norms were found to be increasingly supportive of shoe wearing in the rural community in highland Ethiopia.
Children exhibited greater desire to wear shoes than adults in the rural community in highland Ethiopia.
Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is a disorder characterised by unpredictable seizures, where surgical removal of brain tissue is often the final treatment option.
In roughly 30% of cases, surgery procedures are unsuccessful at preventing future seizures in patients with temporal lobe epilepsy.
The computational model uses patient derived brain connectivity to predict the success rates of surgery in people with temporal lobe epilepsy.
The brains of 22 patients with temporal lobe epilepsy are considered as networks, with brain regions as nodes and the white matter connections between them as edges.
The brain network is unique to each subject and produced from brain imaging scans of 22 patients and 39 controls.
Seizures are simulated before and after surgery in the computational model, where surgery in the model is the removal of nodes from the network.
The computational model successfully identifies regions known to be involved in temporal lobe epilepsy.
The predicted success rates for surgery by the computational model are close to the results found in reality for patients with temporal lobe epilepsy.
The computational model provides patient specific recommendations for surgical procedures, which in simulations show improved results compared to standard surgery in every case.
The application of the computational model is a first step towards designing personalised surgery procedures in order to improve surgery success rates.
Bacteria are surrounded by complex structures called cell envelopes that play an essential role in maintaining cellular integrity.
Organisms classified as Gram-negative have especially complicated envelopes that consist of two membranes with a tough cell wall exoskeleton sandwiched between them.
The envelope architecture of Gram-negative bacteria is extremely proficient at preventing drug molecules from entering the cell.
Gram-negative bacteria are intrinsically resistant to many antibiotics, limiting the therapeutic options for treating infections caused by these organisms.

A quantitative, high-throughput assay for mutants with envelope biogenesis defects was developed to screen an ordered single-gene deletion library of the model Gram-negative bacterium Escherichia coli.
The screen implicated 102 genes of previously unknown function as encoding factors that likely participate in envelope biogenesis in Escherichia coli.
The factor ElyC (YcbC) was characterized further and shown to play a critical role in the metabolism of the essential lipid carrier used for cell wall synthesis in Escherichia coli.
Piwi-interacting small RNAs (piRNAs) protect genome integrity and promote fertility across the animal kingdom.
A conserved sequence motif lies upstream of many piRNA loci in the Caenorhabditis elegans genome and appears to regulate their expression.
More than 70% of piRNAs are differentially enriched in male versus female germline in Caenorhabditis elegans.
Male and female piRNAs in Caenorhabditis elegans show different upstream motifs.

Variation of a single nucleotide within the conserved upstream motif influences piRNA germline enrichment in Caenorhabditis elegans, as demonstrated using a transgenic system for expressing synthetic piRNAs in vivo.
The conserved upstream motif is capable of driving piRNA expression in genomic isolation in Caenorhabditis elegans.
The genomic distribution of conserved upstream motifs determines which sequences are expressed as piRNAs in Caenorhabditis elegans.
Each Caenorhabditis elegans piRNA represents an independent transcript whose sequence, abundance, and germline enrichment are encoded by a variant upstream motif.

The engineered genetic system is based on regulatory RNAs that control the process of protein translation and is able to perform arithmetic logic computations, specifically additions, in a single bacterial cell.
The genetic system expresses fluorescent proteins as output according to the molecular concentrations of the inputs, which are encoded as binary code.
Many genetic variants have been established for diseases, and these findings have raised hope for risk prediction based on genomic profiles.
Proper statistical measures are needed to assess the usefulness of risk prediction tests based on genomic profiles.
This study developed a statistical framework which enables evaluation of many predictive indices analytically.
The statistical framework is based on the liability threshold model, which postulates a latent liability that is normally distributed.
Affected individuals are assumed to have a liability exceeding a certain threshold in the liability threshold model.
Given the overall disease probability and variance in liability explained by genetic markers, a variety of predictive indices can be computed.
The area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, or AUC, is a very commonly employed predictive index.
The limitations of the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, or AUC, are often ignored.

Other computed metrics include the average difference in risks between cases and non-cases, the ability of reclassification into high- and low-risk categories, and the proportion of cases accounted for by a certain percentile of the population at the highest risk.
The study derived how to construct graphs showing the risk distribution in the population.
The phenotypic differences observed between closely related organisms are thought to be due largely to changes in regulatory networks.
Changes in transcriptional networks can occur via mutations in cis binding sites, for which there are numerous known examples.
Changes in transcriptional networks can also occur via binding specificity variation in transcription factors, a less studied phenomenon that has been observed primarily in multi-gene families.
Large-scale experimental studies ascertaining the extent to which transcription factors contribute to regulatory network variation across organisms are lacking and would be time-consuming.
Computational methods can begin to address the challenge of understanding transcription factor contributions to regulatory network variation across organisms.

This study presents a systematic, large-scale analysis of DNA-binding specificity evolution in transcription factor orthologs by computationally leveraging specific features of Cys2-His2 zinc finger proteins, the largest class of transcription factors in animals and major components of their regulatory programs.
Divergence of DNA-binding residues in one-to-one orthologous Cys2-His2 zinc finger proteins is pervasive.
The changes in DNA-binding residues in one-to-one orthologous Cys2-His2 zinc finger proteins show evidence of functional constraint.
The changes in DNA-binding residues in one-to-one orthologous Cys2-His2 zinc finger proteins occur in a gradual, evolutionarily viable manner.
The diversification of orthologous transcription factors has most likely played a major and largely unstudied role in gene regulatory network evolution in metazoans.
Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) decreases the HIV-1 load and reduces mortality due to HIV-1 infection.
HIV-1 establishes latent infection that is resistant to host immune responses and antiretroviral therapy.
HIV-1 latency is the main obstacle to the eradication of the virus from infected patients.
CpG methylation is a mechanism that contributes to transcriptional silencing.
The role of proviral DNA methylation in HIV-1 latency has not been clearly demonstrated and has never been studied in HIV-1-infected patients.
CpG methylation of the HIV-1 promoter is important for the maintenance but not for the establishment of HIV-1 latency in an in vitro model and in HIV-1-infected patients.
Tight control of HIV-1 latency by CpG methylation could be a key barrier to purging the reservoir of latently infected cells in infected individuals.
The heavily methylated promoter/enhancer sequences from latently infected cells make reactivation of HIV-1 difficult.

Addition of some histone deacetylase inhibitors, namely suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid (SAHA), and cytosine methylation inhibitors would represent an important part of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) protocols in the future.
Human immunodeficiency virus type 2 (HIV-2) induces a still poorly understood attenuated infection compared to human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1).

The infection by human immunodeficiency virus type 2 (HIV-2) might follow peculiarities associated with other models of attenuated human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1)/simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) infection, such as a limited infection of a key subset of memory CD4 T lymphocytes, the central-memory ones (TCM).
In peripheral blood cells from 14 untreated human immunodeficiency virus type 2 (HIV-2) infected individuals from the ANRS-CO5 HIV-2 cohort, there was a lack of infection of monocytes.

In peripheral blood cells from 14 untreated human immunodeficiency virus type 2 (HIV-2) infected individuals from the ANRS-CO5 HIV-2 cohort, there was extremely low infection in central-memory CD4+ T lymphocytes while human immunodeficiency virus type 2 (HIV-2) predominated in the transitional-memory cells.
Human immunodeficiency virus type 2 (HIV-2) has a poor replicative capacity in cells from individuals infected with HIV-2.

In central-memory CD4+ T lymphocytes (TCM) from individuals infected with human immunodeficiency virus type 2 (HIV-2), there is a lower expression of CXCR6, a potentially alternative co-receptor of HIV-2 but not of human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1), compared to transitional-memory CD4+ T lymphocytes (TTM).

In central-memory CD4+ T lymphocytes (TCM) from individuals infected with human immunodeficiency virus type 2 (HIV-2), there is a higher expression of TRIM5α, a restriction factor to which human immunodeficiency virus type 2 (HIV-2) is more sensitive than human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1), compared to transitional-memory CD4+ T lymphocytes (TTM).
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the major cause of pneumonia and bronchiolitis among infants and children globally.
In the United States, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections lead to 57,000 hospitalizations among young children, especially in those less than one year old.
Despite the development of immunity following respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection during childhood, individuals remain susceptible to RSV upper respiratory tract reinfection.
The current study explored the antibody repertoires following primary respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection and their evolution in adolescents and adults.

Whole genome-fragment phage display libraries (GFPDL) expressing linear and conformational epitopes from respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) fusion protein (F) and attachment protein (G) were used for unbiased epitope profiling of sera prior to and following RSV infection.
Plasmon Surface Resonance (SPR) was used to measure antibody binding to respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) fusion protein (F) and attachment protein (G) peptides and proteins.
A steady increase in respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) fusion protein (F) epitope repertoires from young children to adults was observed in this study.
Several novel epitopes were identified in pre-fusion respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) fusion protein (F) and an immunodominant epitope was identified in F0-p27 in this study.
For respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) attachment protein (G), antibody responses were high following RSV infection in children but declined in adults.
This study identified unlinked evolution of anti-fusion protein (anti-F) and anti-attachment protein (anti-G) antibody responses to respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).
T cells, an essential component of the immune system, generate protective immune responses against pathogenic organisms and cancer cells.
T cells are produced in the thymus, which provides a unique microenvironment required for T cell development.
Distinct subsets of thymic epithelial cells (TECs) in the outer cortex and inner medulla provide signals required for the survival and differentiation of immature T cells, referred to as thymocytes.
Medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs) play a critical role in preventing autoimmunity because they have the unique ability to express peptides found in other organs throughout the body.
Presentation of self-peptides to thymocytes causes deletion of cells that express high affinity self-reactive receptors.
A major signaling pathway mediated by nuclear factor kappa B (NFκB) family members is indispensable for medullary thymic epithelial cell (mTEC) development.
Signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (Stat3) signaling plays an important role in medullary thymic epithelial cell (mTEC) development and homeostasis.
Constitutive Stat3 activation enhances the survival of immature medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs) and bypasses the requirement for thymocyte-derived signals in medullary region formation.
Stat3 depletion reduces medullary thymic epithelial cell (mTEC) cellularity and impairs medullary region formation.
Chagas disease is the most important vector-borne disease in Latin America.
Residual insecticide spraying has been used successfully for the elimination of domestic vectors in many regions.
Some vectors of non-domestic origin are able to invade houses, and these vectors are now a key challenge for further disease control.
A mathematical model was developed to predict the temporal variations in abundance of non-domiciliated vectors inside houses based on triatomine demographic parameters.
The reliability of the predictions from the mathematical model was demonstrated by comparing these predictions with different sets of insect collection data from the Yucatan peninsula, Mexico.
Vector control strategies based on insecticide spraying, insect screens, and bednets were simulated to evaluate their efficacy at reducing triatomine abundance in houses.

An optimum reduction in bug abundance by at least 80% could be obtained by insecticide application only when doses of at least 50 mg/m2 were applied every year within a two-month period matching the house invasion season by bugs.
The use of insect screens consistently reduced bug abundance in houses and offers a sustainable alternative to insecticide spraying.
Insect screens may be part of novel interventions for the integrated control of various vector-borne diseases.
Plant immunity must be tightly regulated because over- or constitutive activation of plant defenses can cause detrimental effects such as dwarf stature and enhanced cell death.
EDR1, a Raf-like mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) kinase kinase, negatively regulates defenses in Arabidopsis.
The highly conserved mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascades modulate diverse biological processes, including plant immunity.
EDR1 physically associates with MKK4 and MKK5, two mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) kinases, and negatively regulates the protein levels of MKK4, MKK5, MPK3 and MPK6 in Arabidopsis.
EDR1-mediated disease resistance requires MKK4, MKK5 and MPK3 function in Arabidopsis.
Over-expression of MKK4 or MKK5 in wild-type Arabidopsis increased resistance to powdery mildew and caused mildew-induced cell death.
EDR1 negatively regulates defenses and directly modulates the MKK4/MKK5-MPK3/MPK6 cascade to fine-tune plant immunity in Arabidopsis.
The success of a biological event such as cellular adaptation to environmental changes requires the complex process of protein expression to be carried out with high efficiency and fidelity.
Not only transcription but also mRNA homeostasis and translation have to be performed with maximum efficiency to avoid hampering survival.

The role of Elongator, a putative RNA polymerase II (Pol II)-associated complex, in survival to stress is to optimize translation efficiency by modifying some particular transfer RNAs (tRNAs) in this study.
Sin3/Elp3, an Elongator component, participates in the modification of the anticodon of the low copy number tRNALysUUU, which probably favors codon recognition.
The tRNALysUUU recognizes one of the two codons for lysine, which is down-represented in highly expressed constitutive genes.
Stress mRNAs, which are highly expressed upon stress conditions, have not adapted their lysine codon usage from AAA to AAG.
Proper tRNALysUUU modification by Elongator is an alternative strategy to accomplish efficient translation of AAA-containing, abundant stress mRNAs.
Leishmania parasites lodge in host cells within phagolysosome-like structures called parasitophorous vacuoles (PVs).
Depending on the species, amastigote forms can be individually hosted within small, tight-fitting parasitophorous vacuoles (PVs) or grouped within loose, spacious parasitophorous vacuoles (PVs).
Leishmania major parasitophorous vacuoles (PVs) undergo fission as parasites divide in macrophages exposed to Leishmania major amastigotes.
During the course of fission of Leishmania major parasitophorous vacuoles (PVs), there are transients of the lysosomotropic fluorescent probe Lysotracker.

During the course of amastigote population size expansion, Leishmania amazonensis parasitophorous vacuoles (PVs) accumulate Lysotracker while increasing in diameter and volume in macrophages exposed to Leishmania amazonensis amastigotes.
Large Leishmania amazonensis parasitophorous vacuoles (PVs) fuse together, and the products of fusion undergo size and shape remodeling.
The biogenesis and remodeling of the two types of Leishmania parasitophorous vacuoles (PVs) is accompanied by a reduction in the number of macrophage acidic vesicles.
Eukaryotic messenger RNAs (mRNAs) are stabilised by a 5’ cap and one important step in mRNA decay is the removal of this cap by the nudix domain protein Dcp2 of the decapping complex.
The decapping complex is highly conserved throughout eukaryotes, with the exception of trypanosomes that lack the entire complex.
Trypanosomes have evolved to use an ApaH-like phosphatase instead of a nudix domain protein as their major decapping enzyme.
This study reports the first function of an ApaH-like phosphatase, a bacterial derived class of enzymes that are widespread throughout eukaryotes.

Nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) proteins were first identified in plants as disease resistance proteins and were recently found to play essential roles in mammalian innate immunity and inflammation.
NLR protein complexes sense intracellular pathogenic effectors in plants and microbial patterns and danger signals in humans.

Using the Arabidopsis-Pseudomonas interaction as a model system, the molecular link between NLR immune sensors and the convergent immune responses triggered by distinct pathogen effectors was discovered.

Integrated functional genomic and biochemical genetic screens identified six closely related Ca2+-dependent protein kinases (CPKs) that orchestrate bifurcate NLR immune signaling via distinct substrate specificity and subcellular dynamics.
Ca2+-dependent protein kinases CPK1 and CPK2 regulate the onset of programmed cell death in NLR immune signaling.

Ca2+-dependent protein kinases CPK4, CPK5, CPK6, and CPK11 phosphorylate specific WRKY transcription factors to regulate immune gene expression crucial for NLR-dependent restriction of pathogen growth.
Ca2+-dependent protein kinases CPK1, CPK2, CPK4, and CPK11 phosphorylate NADPH oxidases for the production of reactive oxygen species.

Cilia are sensory organelles that are found on most types of human cells and play essential roles in diverse processes ranging from vision and olfaction to embryonic symmetry breaking and kidney development.
Individual cilia are divided into multiple functionally and compositionally distinct compartments, including a proximal "Inversin" compartment, which is located near the base of cilia.
The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, a well-defined animal model of cilia biology, was used to characterize the genetics, components, and defining properties of the proximal cilium.
The Inversin compartment is conserved in Caenorhabditis elegans and is established independent of another proximal ciliary region, the microtubule doublet-based region.

Components of both the microtubule doublet-based region and the Inversin compartment genetically interact to regulate many pathways linked to core aspects of cilia biology, including ciliogenesis, cilia placement, cilia ultrastructure, microtubule stability, and the protein composition of ciliary compartments.
Several of the genes and pathways explored in this study are linked to ciliopathies, a group of diseases caused by dysfunctional cilia.
Sperm cells of animals and lower plants are mobile and can swim to the oocyte or egg cell.

Flowering plants generate immobile sperm encased in a pollen coat to protect the sperm from drying out and the sperm are transported via the pollen tube cell towards the egg apparatus to achieve double fertilization.
Upon arrival the pollen tube tip bursts to deliver two sperm cells, one fusing with the egg cell to generate the embryo and the other fusing with the central cell to generate the endosperm.
Before fertilization the defensin-like protein ZmES1-4 is stored in the secretory zone of the egg apparatus cells in maize.
Pollen tubes cannot discharge sperm in ZmES1-4 knock-down maize plants.
Application of chemically synthesized ZmES4 leads to pollen tube burst within seconds in maize but not in other plant species, suggesting this mechanism may be species specific.
The pollen tube-expressed potassium channel KZM1 is a target of ZmES4 in maize.
The potassium channel KZM1 opens after ZmES4 treatment and probably leads to potassium ion influx and sperm release after osmotic burst in maize.
Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is known to spread both in a cell-free state and from cell to cell.
Design of vaccines attempts to inhibit HIV entry into target cells as do engineered entry inhibitors used as therapeutics.
Neutralizing antibodies and inhibitors block the entry of cell-free HIV particles into cells.
The activity of neutralizing antibodies and inhibitors during cell-cell transmission varies depending on their mode of action.

A prominent class of neutralizing antibodies directed to the CD4 binding site on the HIV envelope very efficiently blocks binding of the virus to its primary receptor on target cells, the CD4 molecule.
Neutralizing antibodies directed to the CD4 binding site on the HIV envelope are elicited in natural infection and once isolated from infected individuals have shown to be highly potent.

CD4 binding site antibodies are dramatically less potent inhibitors of HIV cell-cell transmission and therefore act preferentially by blocking free virus transmission while allowing HIV to spread through cell-cell contact.
Simple models have traditionally been very successful because they usually provide more insight than complicated models.
In physics, simple models can often give highly precise quantitative predictions.
Biology is fundamentally complex and thus it is difficult to find simple models that give precise predictions.
The authors propose to harness the power of deep neural networks but to confine them into modules with a low number of inputs and outputs to create models that are both precise and insightful.
The authors trained one such model to predict the future turning side of a fish in a collective.
By plotting the different modules of the model, the authors obtained insight about how fish interact and how they aggregate information from different neighbours.

The aggregation of information by fish is dynamical and shows that fish can interact with approximately 20 neighbours but can also focus on fewer neighbours, down to 1-2, when some neighbours move at higher speed in front or to the sides, are very close, or are in a collision path.
Exosomes are small membrane-encapsulated vesicles that secrete into the extracellular environment.
Various proteins and RNA molecules have been identified in exosomes whose content reflects the physiological or pathological state of the host cells.

Exosomes released from virus-infected cells contain a variety of viral and host cellular factors that are able to modulate recipient’s cellular responses and result in productive infection of the recipient host.

Enterovirus 71 (EV71), a non-enveloped, single-strand positive sense RNA virus that belongs to the family Picornaviridae and is a major etiologic agent of hand-foot-and-mouth disease (HFMD), could stimulate exosome secretion and differential packaging of the viral genomic RNA and miR-146a into exosomes in this study.

The exosomal viral RNA could be transferred to and replicate in a new target cell while the exosomal miR-146a suppressed type I interferon response in the target cell, thus facilitating the viral replication in this study.
In vivo study showed that exosomal viral RNA exhibited differential tissue accumulation as compared to the free virus particles.
The preferential packaging of miRNA-146a into exosomes is a viral strategy of suppressing host innate immunity upon infection.
The exosomal Enterovirus 71 (EV71) RNA may play an important pathogenic role in the infection.
Malaria infections often consist of more than one strain of the same parasitic species.
Understanding the within-host competition between various strains is essential to understanding the evolution and epidemiology of drug resistance in malarial infections.
The infection process and the competition between strains involve complicated biological processes that are explained by various hypotheses.
Mathematical models tested against experimental data provide quantitative measures to compare hypotheses about the infection process and competition between strains.
Mathematical models tested against experimental data enable researchers to discern the actual biological processes that contribute to the observed dynamics in malaria infections.
The researchers used a group of mathematical models against experimental data on rodent malaria to test various hypotheses.
Quantitative measures in understanding rodent malaria can be considered as a step towards understanding within-host parasite dynamics.
Confronting mathematical models with data allows the discovery of subtle and novel interactions between hosts and parasites that would be impractical to do in an experiment.
Confronting mathematical models with data allows the rejection of hypotheses that are incorrect.
Understanding the forces controlling within-host parasite dynamics in a well-defined experimental model is a necessary step towards understanding these features in natural infections.
A total of 79 asymptomatic visceral leishmaniasis (VL) cases were detected from two kala-azar endemic blocks of Malda districts of West Bengal by active mass screening.
Follow-up study of the asymptomatic visceral leishmaniasis cases revealed that 10.39% of cases transformed into disease.
Follow-up study of the asymptomatic visceral leishmaniasis cases revealed that 9.09% of cases remained sero-positive even after three years.
Progression to clinical disease among asymptomatic individuals was taking place at any time up to three years after the baseline survey.

If there are no cases of visceral leishmaniasis (VL) or post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) for two or more years in a given period, it does not mean that the area is free from leishmaniasis because symptomatic VL or PKDL may appear even after three years if there are asymptomatic cases.
Asymptomatic infected individuals need much attention for the visceral leishmaniasis elimination programme that has been initiated by three adjoining endemic countries.
Eukaryotic genes differ from their prokaryotic counterparts in having intervening non-coding sequences called introns.
The precise biological role of introns in eukaryotic systems remains unclear even more than forty years after their initial discovery.
One function of introns that has been remarkably conserved during evolution is their ability to enhance the transcription of genes that harbor them.
The intron enhances gene expression by affecting direction of the promoter-initiated transcription in this study.
In the presence of an intron, RNA polymerase tends to transcribe the downstream coding region producing messenger RNA (mRNA) in this study.
In the absence of a splicing-competent intron, RNA polymerase starts transcribing the promoter upstream region producing upstream antisense RNA (uaRNA) in this study.
Intron-mediated promoter directionality was dependent on gene looping, which is the interaction of the promoter and terminator region of a gene in a transcription-dependent manner in this study.
The intron-dependent gene looping facilitates the recruitment of termination factors in the promoter-proximal region in this study.
The recruited termination factors stop upstream antisense RNA (uaRNA) synthesis thereby conferring directionality to the promoter-bound RNA polymerase in this study.
The molecular evolution of any organism is described by changes in the genotype resulting from genetic drift or selection to maintain or establish fitness under the given environmental conditions.
Identification of phenotype-defining changes and their distinction from near-neutral 'hitchhiker' changes is a fundamental challenge in genome research.
The standard approach to identifying phenotype-defining changes involves time- and cost-intensive mutation experiments, which are typically low throughput due to their experimental nature.

The authors have developed a computational method for the inference of phenotypic impact of genotypic changes that is applicable to any system, within or across species, where homologous genetic sequences and associated pairwise phenotype distances are available.
The authors demonstrated the accuracy of their computational method by application to the human influenza A (H3N2) virus.

Recognizing changes in the antigenic phenotype and a viral strain's capability to evade pre-existing host immunity is important for the production of efficient vaccines against the human influenza A (H3N2) virus.
The authors accurately identified known sites and amino acid changes with antigenic impact over 35 years of evolution of the human influenza A (H3N2) virus.
There exists a superabundance of human sequence variations.

Testing every sequence variant for association with human disease is often infeasible because studies must be very large and expensive to overcome the statistical penalties used to control for multiple tests.
A common alternative is to assay only a subset of sequence variants for which there are prior reasons to believe they may be disease-causing.
Sequence variants that change conserved amino acids are often disease-causing.
Variants that occur at homologous positions within paralogous human proteins can be used as a means of identifying disease-causing DNA sequence variations.

DNA sequence variants co-occur at aligned amino acid pairs more frequently than expected by chance, suggesting that similar functional constraints on paralogous proteins result in coordinated distributions of variants along their lengths.
If one member of a variant-pair is disease-causing, its partner is likely to be disease-causing as well.
All positive-strand RNA viruses replicate their genomes in association with host cell membranes.
Poliovirus induces membranes with unique structure and lipid composition rather than just remodeling existing membranes.
There has been some suggestion that the functions of the poliovirus-induced structures observed during infection may not be those that perform genome replication.

Kinetic analysis and kinetic traps of virus-induced membrane formation/transformation and phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate (PI4P) induction by wild-type poliovirus and two poliovirus mutants provide evidence for the existence of a virus-induced genome-replication organelle temporally and spatially distinct from a virus-assembly organelle.
Formation of both the virus-induced genome-replication organelle and the virus-assembly organelle may require participation of poliovirus viral proteins 3AB and/or 3CD.

Seasonal influenza A viruses (IAV) cause tens of thousands of deaths and tens of billions of dollars in economic costs every year in the United States alone, despite widespread pre-exposure and vaccination.
Influenza A virus (IAV) persists within the human population by evading herd immunity through the continual accumulation of immune escape substitutions in a process known as antigenic drift.
The specific mechanisms that facilitate influenza A virus (IAV) antigenic drift remain unclear, making it difficult to design more efficacious, escape-proof vaccines.

A high-definition population sequencing approach was used to understand how influenza A virus (IAV) tolerates the accumulation of immune escape substitutions during antigenic drift without losing fitness.
The influenza A virus (IAV) rapidly acquired N-linked glycan structures on the hemagglutinin (HA) protein following escape from a panel of neutralizing antibodies.
Glycosylation of the hemagglutinin (HA) protein alleviated the deleterious effects of immune escape substitutions on interactions with host cell receptors in influenza A virus (IAV).
Madurella mycetomatis mycetoma is a chronic fungal infection that frequently results in mutilating lesions.
The causative agents of Madurella mycetomatis mycetoma are found in soil.
Many people are exposed to the causative agents of Madurella mycetomatis mycetoma but most do not develop mycetoma.
The fungus Madurella mycetomatis organizes itself in a grain once inside the body in patients with mycetoma.
The grain formed by Madurella mycetomatis in the body contains chitin.
The immune system of the host tries to eliminate the grains formed by Madurella mycetomatis by producing cytokines and enzymes, including the chitin-degrading chitinases.
Human chitinases acidic mammalian chitinase (AMCase) and chitotriosidase bind to fungal chitin in the grain formed by Madurella mycetomatis.
A polymorphism in the gene for chitotriosidase that results in enzyme inactivity is associated with increased risk for Madurella mycetomatis mycetoma.
Chitotriosidase is important in the pathogen-eliminating immune response that results in clearance of Madurella mycetomatis infection.
The absence of chitotriosidase results in increased acidic mammalian chitinase (AMCase) production and thus in grain formation in Madurella mycetomatis mycetoma.
The development of Madurella mycetomatis mycetoma is multifactorial and other factors besides chitotriosidase polymorphisms also play a role.
Folliculogenesis is a progressive and highly regulated process that requires the tight coordination of metabolism and bidirectional communication between the oocyte and granulosa cells.
Geranylgeranyl diphosphate (GGPP)-mediated protein geranylgeranylation, a post-translational modification, is essential for the oocyte-granulosa cell communication in this study.
GGPP depletion in oocytes inhibits Rho GTPase geranylgeranylation-regulated cell adhesion in this study.
GGPP depletion in oocytes impairs Rab GTPase geranylgeranylation-directed cell secretion in this study.

The inhibition of Rho GTPase geranylgeranylation-regulated cell adhesion and impairment of Rab GTPase geranylgeranylation-directed cell secretion caused by GGPP depletion in oocytes are responsible for the failure to maintain oocyte-granulosa cell communication in this study.

The failure to maintain oocyte-granulosa cell communication caused by GGPP depletion in oocytes probably cannot support the proliferation of granulosa cells from one layer to multiple layers in this study.

The failure to maintain oocyte-granulosa cell communication caused by GGPP depletion in oocytes ultimately results in the failure of the primary-secondary follicle transition and female subfertility in this study.
GGPP-mediated protein geranylgeranylation is involved in regulating the primary-secondary follicle transition in this study.
GGPP-mediated protein geranylgeranylation establishes a novel link between folliculogenesis and GGPP-regulated membrane dynamics in this study.
Social isolation severely affects the behavior and physiology of social animals, including humans.
The fruit fly is a powerful model for studying the mechanisms of development, health and disease and is also used to study social behaviors such as mating and aggression.

Previous studies of social behaviors in fruit flies are limited to examining few individuals for short amounts of time due to the lack of effective computational tools for the analysis of large groups over prolonged time.
The researchers built a new behavioral arena and developed new software that accurately tracks many fruit flies simultaneously over long time periods.
The new behavioral arena is cheap and easy to build and the new software works with low resolution videos.
Using the improved tools, the researchers studied social isolation in groups of male fruit flies.
Social isolation caused fruit flies to form stronger interactions with neighboring flies in their social network.
The behavioral changes caused by social isolation in fruit flies were preceded by transient changes in the expression of metabolism genes.
Social isolation eventually resulted in isolated fruit flies accumulating fat, as has been previously observed in studies in mice and humans.
The study enables the use of fruit flies in future studies of social isolation.
This study presents the first example of prion strains that replicate independently in vitro and in vivo.
The observation that prion strains replicate independently in vitro and in vivo changes the paradigm of the interactions of prion strains.
The observation that prion strains replicate independently in vitro and in vivo provides further evidence that prion strains are a dynamic mixture of substrains.
Strain interference is influenced by the abundance of cellular prion protein (PrPC) that is convertible by the prion strains involved.
The observations about prion strain replication and interference have implications for interspecies transmission and emergence of prion strains from a mixture.
The proposed model is based directly on insect neuroanatomy and is able to account for the route following capabilities of ants.
The mushroom body circuit in the proposed model has the potential to store a large number of images generated in a realistic simulation of an ant traversing a route.
The mushroom body circuit in the proposed model can distinguish previously stored images from highly similar images generated when looking in the wrong direction.
The mushroom body circuit in the proposed model can control successful recapitulation of routes under ecologically valid test conditions.
A key event in regulating gene expression involves changes in the acetylation status of core histones.
Regulation of histone acetylation is accomplished by a balance between the addition of acetyl groups by histone acetyltransferase enzymes and removal of the moieties by deacetylases.
Changes in histone acetylation are essential in regulating cellular differentiation and proliferation.
Disruption of changes in histone acetylation results in a variety of pathologies, including cancer.
Histone acetylation regulators are targeted by herpesviruses to ensure persistent infection during the life of the host.
In the case of the herpesvirus human cytomegalovirus (HCMV), changes in histone acetylation have been implicated in the choice between latent and acute phases of infection.
A focused proteomics approach was used to identify proteins that interact with and regulate the histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1) protein during acute cytomegalovirus infection.
The studies identified numerous cellular and viral proteins including human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) pUL29/28.
The human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) pUL29/28 protein binds to components of the nucleosome remodeling and deacetylase complex, NuRD.
Functional nucleosome remodeling and deacetylase complex (NuRD) components are necessary for human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) gene expression and infection.

The study demonstrates a new tool for studying host-pathogen interactions and provides new insights into the complex regulation of histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1) during human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) replication.
Black Sigatoka or black leaf streak disease, caused by the ascomycete fungus Pseudocercospora fijiensis, inflicts huge costs on banana producers due to crop losses and expenses for disease control.
The global banana export trade relies on Cavendish clones that are highly susceptible to Pseudocercospora fijiensis.
Sustainable production of the world’s number one fruit requires a better understanding of host resistance and sophisticated management of fungicide resistance in the pathogen.

In the Pseudocercospora fijiensis genome sequence, the researchers identified an effector that induced a hypersensitive response-like necrosis on a resistant banana accession but not on a susceptible cultivar.
The assay based on the effector inducing hypersensitive response-like necrosis may be useful for identifying resistance in banana breeding programs if validated.
The researchers used the Pseudocercospora fijiensis genomic sequence to develop highly polymorphic molecular markers for analyzing Pseudocercospora fijiensis field populations.
There is a strong enrichment of nearly 100% for fungicide resistance markers in fungicide-treated banana plantations compared to untreated wild-type populations of Pseudocercospora fijiensis.
The rapid evolution of fungicide resistance in Pseudocercospora fijiensis poses an immediate threat to sustainable banana production.

Human papillomaviruses (HPV), which comprise more than 100 genotypes, are the most prevalent sexually transmitted infection and are associated with multiple human cancers including all cervical cancers, many other anogenital cancers, and 25% of head and neck cancers.

The human papillomavirus (HPV) life cycle is closely linked to epithelial differentiation of skin keratinocytes, with initial infection occurring only in the undifferentiated proliferating basal compartment of the epithelium and progeny virus production only in the terminally differentiated suprabasal compartment.
Cell cycle progression through mitosis is critical for the establishment of human papillomavirus (HPV) infection in this study that identified small molecule inhibitors of HPV infection.
Early steps of mitosis are required for human papillomavirus (HPV) infection and early gene expression according to the chemical genetic dissection performed in this study.

The human brain is theorised to operate like a sophisticated hypothesis tester, using past experience to generate a model of the external world, testing predictions of this model against incoming sensory evidence, and generating a ‘prediction error’ signal that updates the model when predictions and sensory evidence do not match.
An optimal system should predict the reliability (or ‘precision’) of sensory signals to minimise the influence of unreliable sensory information.
Attention optimises the process of prediction by boosting prediction error signals, which are coded as the difference (or ‘mismatch’) between predicted and observed stimulus features.
This theory predicts that attention should increase the selectivity for mismatch information in the neural response to surprising stimuli.

In a study with human participants, a decoding algorithm was trained to identify ‘mismatch information’ in the brain recorded by electroencephalography (EEG) following the presentation of surprising stimuli that were either attended or ignored.

Attention increased the selectivity for mismatch information in the neural response to surprising stimuli in human participants, supporting the notion that attention and prediction are intricately related processes.

Robust lineage decisions in developmental biology are implemented by genetic switches, whereby one set of master genes are ON and another set are OFF, leading to a specific expression pattern of genes for a particular lineage.

The computational model developed in this study illustrates principles applied to the hematopoietic erythroid-myeloid lineage choice, where two master regulator genes, PU.1 and GATA-1, function as a genetic switch.

The computational model, which is based upon known interactions, suggests missing interactions between the master genes PU.1 and GATA-1, which the authors hypothesize to reproduce the desired dynamics.
There exist feedback interactions between the master genes PU.1 and GATA-1 and their downstream targets.

When feedback interactions between the master genes PU.1 and GATA-1 and their downstream targets are included in the model, the dynamics imply that the feedback is responsible for irreversible commitment.
The results of the computational model suggest searching for missing interactions between the master genes PU.1 and GATA-1 in terms of a coregulated cofactor.
Reprogramming irreversible cell fate may be possible by perturbing feedback regulation between the master genes PU.1 and GATA-1 and their downstream targets according to the computational model.
Dynamical modeling provides prediction of novel mechanisms and strategies for reprogramming the fates of cells.
Proteins are responsible for much of the biological ‘heavy lifting’ that keeps human cells functioning.
Proteins typically bind together to form geometrically and chemically complex structures that are tailored for a specific task.
Experimental techniques allow researchers to detect whether two types of proteins are capable of binding together, or ‘interacting’.
Protein-protein interaction networks have been developed for several organisms using a range of methods, all of which are subject to experimental errors.
Protein-protein interaction network data reveal a fascinating and intricate pattern of connections.
Proteins can be arranged into a low-dimensional space, such as a three-dimensional cube, so that interacting proteins are close together.

The authors' work shows that the low-dimensional structure of protein-protein interaction networks can be exploited to assign confidence levels to recorded protein-protein interactions and predict new interactions that were overlooked experimentally.
In tests, the authors predicted 251 new human protein-protein interactions.
Through literature curation, the authors independently validated a statistically significant number of the predicted new human protein-protein interactions.
A new variant form of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease was identified a decade ago.
The emergence of the new variant form of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in humans was the consequence of the zoonotic transmission of bovine spongiform encephalopathy through dietary exposure.
A policy based on the exclusion of known infectious materials from the food chain has been implemented to control human exposure to prions.
All investigations carried out failed to reveal evidence of infectivity in milk from affected ruminants.
Milk from affected ruminants has continuously been considered as safe because investigations failed to reveal evidence of infectivity in this milk.
This study demonstrates the presence of prions in colostrum and milk from sheep incubating natural scrapie and displaying apparently healthy mammary glands.
Milk from small ruminants could contribute to the transmission of prion disease between animals.
Milk products from ovine and other dairy species raise some concern with regard to the risk to humans associated with prion disease.
Approximately a half-billion people worldwide are infected with herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), the virus that causes genital herpes.
In some individuals, herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) infection results in painful, recurrent genital ulcers.
In some individuals, herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) infection remains quiescent.
In both symptomatic and asymptomatic settings, individuals infected with herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) may transmit the virus to their intimate partners.
Genital herpes increases the risk that an infected person will acquire human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) if exposed during sexual intercourse.
A vaccine for the prevention of genital herpes is a high priority.

The described vaccine induces antibodies that block the ability of herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) to enter cells and prevents the virus from escaping immune attack mediated by antibody and complement.
The vaccine contains herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) glycoproteins C, D, and E and is immunogenic in non-human primates.
The vaccine protects immunized non-human primates against a mild vaginal infection that develops in naïve animals after intravaginal inoculation of herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2).

Naïve guinea pigs develop severe genital disease after intravaginal infection with herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), while immunized guinea pigs are almost 100% protected after intravaginal infection.

The vaccine greatly reduces the number of days during the recurrent phase of herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) infection that animals shed virus in genital secretions, thereby reducing the risk of transmission.
The described novel vaccine is a leading candidate for clinical trials aimed at preventing genital herpes infection in humans.
Chemotaxis of bacteria plays an important role in their life by providing bacteria with the ability to actively search for an optimal growth environment.
The chemotaxis system is highly optimized because on the evolutionary time scale even a modest enhancement of its efficiency can give cells a large competitive advantage.
For a long time it was believed that the only navigation mechanism of bacteria is increasing the run length toward the preferred direction.
The tumble was assumed to be a purely random change of direction between runs.
Recently published experimental data demonstrate a dependence of tumbling angle on the number of clockwise (CW)-switched motors in bacteria.

The authors introduced the dependence of tumbling angle on the number of clockwise (CW)-switched motors into their model of chemotactic Escherichia coli (E. coli) and simulated it under different conditions.

Simulations show that the dependence of tumbling angle on the number of clockwise (CW)-switched motors is an important additional mechanism of bacterial navigation that was previously unrecognized because it lies below the experimental errors of conventional single-cell tracking.
Fine tuning of tumbling significantly improves the efficiency of chemotaxis and represents a new level of evolutionary optimization of bacteria.
In aquatic animal swimming, the Strouhal number specifies the frequency of fin movement for maximum propulsive efficiency in animals that use the common body/caudal fin swimming mode, such as trout.
Median/paired fin swimming is a widespread form of locomotion used by animals as diverse as cuttlefish, triggerfish, and rays.
The optimal specific wavelength determines the wavelength of fin movement required for maximum propulsive force or thrust in median/paired fin swimming.

Adherence to the optimal specific wavelength has independently emerged within eight clades of animals in three different phyla, including vertebrates and invertebrates, encompassing over a thousand species.
Many large-scale mathematical models describe metabolism to understand how microbes and other organisms, including humans, function and interact with each other and with their environment.

Making large-scale mathematical models of metabolism is extremely time- and effort-intensive because it requires gathering and combining information from many sources, including the organism’s genome sequence, biological databases, scientific literature, and expert advice.

The exact procedure and resources used to create large-scale mathematical models of metabolism depend on the model creators’ expertise and research interests, resulting in independently created models for the same organism that are often very different and can hardly be compared.
Each independently created large-scale mathematical model of metabolism typically contains unique information that is lost when working with a different model.
The computational tool COMMGEN was developed to build consensus metabolic models by integrating the available knowledge from independently generated models.
COMMGEN combines independently generated metabolic models by matching identical parts and resolving differences between inconsistent parts.
COMMGEN was applied to four sets of models of different organisms.
In all four sets of models of different organisms, COMMGEN identified and resolved hundreds of inconsistencies.
COMMGEN can be generally applied to standardize and improve models of metabolism, particularly for complex scenarios such as those involving microbial communities and host-pathogen interactions.
A global programme aims to eliminate Gambian sleeping sickness (Human African Trypanosomiasis, HAT) as a public health problem by 2020.
Gambian Human African Trypanosomiasis is a neglected tropical disease caused by trypanosomes spread by tsetse flies.
Control of Gambian Human African Trypanosomiasis has relied largely on detection and treatment of human cases.

In the Mandoul focus of southern Chad, regular screening of the human population of approximately 39,000 people between 2002 and 2013 resulted in the detection and treatment of approximately 100 cases per year.
In February 2014, 2,600 insecticide-treated targets called ‘Tiny Targets’ were deployed in areas where tsetse flies were present.
Tsetse flies are attracted to the insecticide-treated ‘Tiny Targets’ and pick up a lethal dose of insecticide upon contacting the targets.

Monitoring of the tsetse population using a network of 44 traps operated regularly between November 2013 and October 2016 showed that the mean daily catch of tsetse declined by 99.99%, from 0.7 tsetse per trap before targets were deployed to 0.005 tsetse per trap.
The number of Human African Trypanosomiasis cases detected by a programme of active screening declined during the period between November 2013 and October 2016.
Mathematical modelling of the number of Human African Trypanosomiasis cases reported during 2000–2015 suggests that 70% of the decline in cases during 2014–2015 was due to vector control.

Mathematical modelling suggests that the combination of case detection, treatment, and vector control may have interrupted transmission and may lead to the elimination of sleeping sickness in the Mandoul focus by 2020.

The results from Mandoul provide empirical and theoretical evidence that the global elimination of Gambian Human African Trypanosomiasis can be achieved through the integrated use of case detection and treatment and vector control.
Mucosal histology plays a key role in the diagnosis, characterization, and propagation of a host of gastrointestinal diseases.
Inflammation is a significant factor in the pathogenesis of a series of gastrointestinal diseases.
Inflammation affects the maintenance of the mucosal architecture by morphogenic pathways.
The Spatially Explicit General-purpose Model of Enteric Tissue (SEGMEnT) was developed to investigate the behavior of enteric epithelial tissue as influenced by inflammation.
SEGMEnT integrates cellular and molecular pathways governing morphogenesis and inflammation to generate a variety of pathophysiological processes from a common platform and knowledge base.
SEGMEnT reproduces healthy and disease ileal mucosal dynamics.
SEGMEnT provides insight into a range of clinically relevant cellular-molecular mechanisms.
Phosphotase and tensin homolog/phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PTEN/PI3K) has a novel putative role as a key point of crosstalk between enteric inflammation and morphogenesis.
Enterocyte sloughing has a protective role in enteric ischemia-reperfusion.
Chronic low level inflammation acts as a driver for colonic metaplasia.
SEGMEnT can serve as an integrating platform for the study of inflammation in gastrointestinal disease.
The evolutionarily conserved Wnt/Wingless signal transduction pathway regulates cell proliferation and cell fate specification during animal development and tissue homeostasis.
Deregulation of Wnt signaling triggers the development of nearly all colorectal cancers and is associated with several other diseases.
Wnt ligands are secreted from the cells in which they are produced and move from there to distant cells.
The movement of Wnt ligands to distant cells is controversial regarding its essentiality for Wnt function in cell fate specification.

The researchers utilized a genetic model in the Drosophila adult intestine, which is subdivided into compartments with distinct anatomy, physiology, functional roles, cell types, and gene expression patterns, similar to its mammalian counterpart.
Wingless, the primary Drosophila Wnt ligand, is expressed and activates signaling at each major intestinal compartment boundary to specify cell fate.
Wingless is required for many processes in the development of the adult Drosophila intestine.
The ability of Wingless to move from its site of synthesis and act at long range is essential for the development of the adult Drosophila intestine.
The ability of Wingless to signal at long range is critical for tissue formation and function, with relevance for animal development and human disease.
Trypanosomiasis is a major health threat in Africa.
Vaccine development for trypanosomiasis has long been hampered by the extraordinarily diverse surface proteins of Trypanosoma parasites.
Serengeti lions show an asymptotic age prevalence of the non-pathogenic Trypanosoma congolense.
Serengeti lions show a strong peak and decrease in age prevalence of the pathogenic Trypanosoma brucei sensu lato.
The pattern of age prevalence in Serengeti lions suggests that lions may gain cross-immunity to Trypanosoma brucei from repeated exposure to the more genetically diverse Trypanosoma congolense.
Lions may gain more effective cross immunity than other host species owing to their frequent consumption of infected prey animals.
The findings about cross-immunity in lions suggest possible strategies for designing effective vaccines against sleeping sickness in livestock and humans.
When a species is grown under optimal conditions, the single-knockout of most of its genes is not likely to affect its viability.
The resilience of biological systems to mutations is termed genetic robustness.

The extent of species' genetic robustness reflects both the range of conditions in which the species can survive and the availability of alternative cellular routes compensating for a gene's loss of function.
The authors developed a computational model for estimating the essentiality of metabolic reactions across natural-like environments and applied it to chart species' level of genetic robustness.

Studying robustness across a wide collection of natural-like environments enables stratification, for each species individually, of the extent of environmental-dependent and environmental-independent robustness.
The level of environmental-dependent robustness is associated with the lifestyle of a species, such as being a specialist or a generalist.
The level of environmental-independent robustness is associated with the metabolic production capacities of a species.
The human herpesvirus Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is an important human pathogen involved in infectious mononucleosis and several malignant tumors, including lymphomas in immunosuppressed patients.
Upon primary infection, a balance between Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and the host is established, to which EBV’s capacity to dodge T cell-mediated attack contributes.
The Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) late protein gp150 acts as a novel immunoevasin that frustrates antigen presentation by human leukocyte antigen (HLA) class I, class II, and CD1d molecules.
Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) gp150’s many sialoglycans create a shield that impedes surface detection of presented antigen.
Exploiting glycan shielding as a mechanism to mask surface-exposed proteins on infected cells could permit Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) to additionally modulate other aspects of host antiviral defense.
B cells producing wild-type Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) escaped immune recognition more efficiently than B cells infected with a gp150-null virus in this study.
Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) gp150 blocks antigen presentation to T cells through glycan shielding, representing a novel, broadly active strategy of herpesvirus immune evasion.
Bipolar disorder (BD) is a highly heritable disease that has been difficult to characterize genetically.
The researchers genotyped 1,190 bipolar disorder (BD) cases and 401 controls to find regions of the genome associated with bipolar disorder.
After combining the new genotyped data with previously existing genotyped samples, the researchers did not find any genome-wide significant associations with bipolar disorder.

When the researchers used an additional study to prioritize loci for replication and meta-analysis purposes, they found that they were more likely to see an association in their sample with variants for which they had the highest power.

The researchers quantified the effect of power to detect an effect based on an initial study's results on replication P-value in a second study using logistic regression and found a strong association with P = 1.5×10−7.
The association between power to detect an effect and replication P-value was stronger when the analysis was restricted to single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) near coding regions.
The association was further enriched when single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) had the same direction of effect in both studies.
The results support the presence of genetic factors underlying bipolar disorder near exons whose collective effect results in a detectable signal.
The results provide a framework for assessing the potential for replication when combining results from multiple studies.
Cyanobacteria filaments are paradigmatic examples of prokaryotic cellular differentiation and cooperative pattern formation.
When a cyanobacteria filament is deprived of combined nitrogen, some vegetative cells differentiate into heterocysts, which are terminally differentiated nitrogen-fixing cells.
Most cells in a cyanobacteria filament do not differentiate but remain in their initial vegetative state.

The coexistence of heterocysts and vegetative cells is essential for the survival of the cyanobacteria filament because heterocysts lose their photosynthetic capacity and need vegetative cells to provide a source of fixed carbon.
Cell division, i.e. reproduction, in cyanobacteria filaments is only accomplished by vegetative cells.

Differentiation processes in cyanobacteria filaments result from the interplay of complex regulatory networks acting inside the cell and external stimuli coming from both adjacent cells and the environment.
American visceral leishmaniasis (VL) can lead to death in 5-10% of patients under treatment in Latin America.
The fatality rates associated with American visceral leishmaniasis (VL) have remained stable at a high level over the years in Brazil.
Fatality rates associated with American visceral leishmaniasis (VL) are not recorded in under-treatment patients from endemic countries of the Old World.
Fatality rates associated with American visceral leishmaniasis (VL) are not recorded in under-treatment patients from non-endemic countries where such cases are imported.
Lethality induced by American visceral leishmaniasis (VL) can occur even after the implementation of recommended therapy.

Understanding individual, clinical, and laboratory factors that predispose to an unfavorable outcome might represent an important feature for informing better practice in the clinical management of American visceral leishmaniasis (VL) cases.
The present systematic review with meta-analysis brings together information on various prognostic variables associated with the severity of American visceral leishmaniasis (VL).
Thirteen potential predictors of severity in American visceral leishmaniasis (VL) were considered to be of significant relevance based on the strength of evidence available in the studies surveyed.
There are gaps in the existing knowledge and a need for the development of externally validated prognostic models for American visceral leishmaniasis (VL).
The results of the systematic review and meta-analysis could be useful in identifying patients at higher risk of unfavorable evolution or death from American visceral leishmaniasis (VL).
The results of the systematic review and meta-analysis might provide an aid in decision-making regarding the clinical management of American visceral leishmaniasis (VL) cases.
The cells of living organisms do not concurrently express their entire complement of genes.
Cells regulate their gene expression, which allows different cells to adopt different stable gene expression patterns.
The development of an embryo necessitates that cells alter their gene expression patterns in order to differentiate.
Gene expression phenotypes are largely robust to genetic mutation in living organisms.
One source of robustness to genetic mutation in gene expression phenotypes may reside in the network structure of interacting molecules that underlie genetic regulation.
Theoretical studies of regulatory networks have linked network structure to robustness.
It is necessary to more extensively characterize real-world regulatory networks in order to understand which structural properties may be biologically meaningful.
The authors recently used theoretical models to show that a particular structural property, degree assortativity, is linked to robustness.
The authors measured the assortativity of human regulatory networks in 41 distinct cell and tissue types.
The authors developed a theoretical framework to explore how degree assortativity affects robustness.
The gene expression phenotypes of human regulatory networks are more robust than expected by chance alone.
Cellular reaction networks show a substantial degree of complexity, and many of the regulatory mechanisms in cellular reaction networks are yet to be discovered.
Building detailed mathematical models of complete cellular reaction networks is not only unrewarding but most often impossible.
Focus is put on small subnetworks such as the transcriptional circuitry associated with a few genes instead of modeling complete cellular reaction networks.
Small subnetworks such as the transcriptional circuitry associated with a few genes are still embedded in the cellular environment and are consequently modulated by the cellular environment.
The mathematical framework presented in this work allows building models of small subnetworks only, while still incorporating the impact of the cellular environment.

Models of small subnetworks that incorporate the impact of the cellular environment are instrumental for advancing biological understanding and for the reliable forward engineering of new subnetworks in synthetic biology.
Human zinc-finger antiviral protein (ZAP) is a cellular restriction factor against many viruses.
The role of human zinc-finger antiviral protein (ZAP) with regard to the flavivirus family is largely unknown.
Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) is sensitive to human zinc-finger antiviral protein (ZAP) in this study.
Dengue virus and Zika virus are resistant to human zinc-finger antiviral protein (ZAP) in this study.
Human zinc-finger antiviral protein (ZAP) specifically targets Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) viral RNA and induces translation repression and RNA degradation in this study.

The findings of this study highlight the human zinc-finger antiviral protein (ZAP)-mediated anti-Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) mechanisms and extend the antiviral spectrum of human zinc-finger antiviral protein (ZAP) to include a member of the Flavivirus genus.
The mammalian host triggers a complex cascade of events upon a bacterial infection to prevent pathogen-induced damage.
Many bacterial pathogens are successfully eliminated by the host immune system.
Some bacterial pathogens, including enteric yersiniae, have evolved strategies to efficiently evade immune surveillance.
The evasion of immune surveillance enables enteric yersiniae to colonize specific sites in the host where they can persist for years.
Persistent infections by enteric yersiniae are often asymptomatic for long time periods but can undergo reactivation and cause clinical symptoms.
The study investigated changes of bacterial and host responses from an acute to a persistent infection to understand how enteric bacteria can persist in gut-associated host niches.

Persistency of Yersinia pseudotuberculosis in the cecum is characterized by suppression of pathogen-induced inflammation and tissue destruction, and an induction of interferon-gamma promoted tolerogenic responses.
Removal of a single bacterial virulence factor, the CNFY toxin, can trigger the process of persistency and drives Yersinia pseudotuberculosis into persistency.
When active, the enzyme cyclin B1–cyclin-dependent kinase 1 (Cdk1) commits a growing cell to the process of mitotic cell division and chromosome separation.
Cyclin B1–Cdk1 activation is controlled in many ways, but once cyclin B1–Cdk1 activity rises above a certain level, further activation of cyclin B1–Cdk1 is catalyzed by a positive-feedback loop.
The positive-feedback loop generates highly active cyclin B1–Cdk1 and triggers the start of mitosis, which can only be completed when cyclin B1–Cdk1 activity is properly shut off again.
It is not clear how cyclin B1–Cdk1 activity develops in human cells or how the switch between cyclin B1–Cdk1 inactive and active states is controlled.
The study combines activation measurements with a kinetic model to study how cyclin B1–Cdk1 activity accumulates just before and during mitosis.
Cyclin B1–Cdk1 activity develops gradually in early mitosis in human cells.
Different cyclin B1–Cdk1 activity levels are required for initiation of, and progression through, mitosis in human cells.
Once cyclin B1–Cdk1 activation is truly launched, cyclin B1–Cdk1 activation is bound to continue and will not lightly drop back again.
The successive cyclin B1–Cdk1 activity levels by themselves may coordinate the progression through the distinct phases of mitosis.
Filarial nematodes are a group of pathogenic helminth parasites that include those responsible for the diseases lymphatic filariasis and onchocerciasis.
Filarial nematodes have evolved a mutualistic association with the intracellular bacterial symbiont Wolbachia, providing a novel approach to their treatment and control using antibiotics.
Depletion of Wolbachia leads to a rapid and sustained induction of cell death through apoptosis of reproductive cells, developing embryos, microfilariae, and developing larvae in filarial nematodes.
Apoptosis affects embryonic cells other than those infected with Wolbachia bacteria in filarial nematodes.
The Wolbachia populations in the adult hypodermis of filarial nematodes, rather than the few bacteria present in the developing embryos, are essential to avoid apoptosis.

The mode of action of antibiotic treatment of filarial nematodes includes induction of apoptosis, which accounts for some of the key anti-filarial activities and identifies one of the biological processes underlying the mutualistic symbiosis between filarial nematodes and Wolbachia.
A mind-blowing diversity of sex-determining mechanisms exists among eukaryotes.
Highly differentiated sex chromosomes consist of a degenerate, gene-poor Y chromosome and an often dosage-compensated X chromosome and appear to represent an evolutionary dead-end.
Dipteran insects, which include flies and mosquitoes, are generally considered to have stable XY sex chromosomes.
A whole-genome analysis of 37 fly species from 22 families of Diptera uncovers tremendous hidden variation in sex chromosomes.
Some fly species have newly gained or secondarily lost their sex chromosomes.
In some fly species, a different chromosome has replaced the original sex chromosome.
In some fly species, multiple chromosomal elements have become incorporated into the sex chromosomes.
Some fly species have female heterogametic sex chromosomes.
A comparative transcriptome analysis shows that dosage compensation has evolved multiple times in dipteran insects.
Dosage compensation in dipteran insects has consistently evolved through up-regulation of the single X chromosome in males.
Diverse fly species provide a rich resource to study sex chromosome biology in a comparative manner.
Similar selective forces have shaped the unique evolution of sex chromosomes in diverse fly taxa.
The bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa produces the long sugar polymer alginate as a defense mechanism.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa uses the polymer alginate to form a biofilm that acts as a barrier to protect against antibiotics and the host immune response.
During its biosynthesis, alginate undergoes a chemical modification whereby acetate is added to the polymer.
Acetylation of alginate makes the bacterial biofilm less susceptible to recognition and clearance by the host immune system.
AlgJ is one of four proteins required for O-acetylation of the alginate polymer.
AlgJ is structurally similar to AlgX, which is also required for alginate acetylation.
AlgJ exhibits acetylesterase activity by catalyzing the removal of acetyl groups from a surrogate substrate.
AlgJ does not bind to short mannuronic acid polymers.
AlgX binds alginate in a length-dependent manner and is capable of transferring acetate from a surrogate substrate onto alginate.

The absence of infective larvae of Onchocerca volvulus in the black fly vector and reduction of exposure to and new infections with Onchocerca volvulus are the criteria currently used to certify focal interruption of parasite transmission.
Entomological and epidemiological assessments in the Southern Chiapas focus of Mexico indicate that transmission of Onchocerca volvulus has been interrupted in this focus.

None of the Simulium ochraceum sensu lato vector black flies collected from sentinel and extra-sentinel communities in the Southern Chiapas focus during the 2011 transmission season was found to contain Onchocerca volvulus parasite DNA when tested by polymerase chain reaction-enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (PCR-ELISA), suggesting vector parasite contact was nearly nonexistent.
There was minimal exposure to Onchocerca volvulus in children 5 years of age and under in the Southern Chiapas focus, as measured by circulating antibody to a parasite-specific antigen.

The Southern Chiapas focus was the major focus of Onchocerca volvulus transmission in Mexico and one of the largest in Latin America, with a well-documented history of active transmission prior to the commencement of Mectizan mass distribution.
This study demonstrates the interruption of Onchocerca volvulus transmission in a geographically large focus in Latin America with a historically high intensity of transmission.
The centrosomes are responsible for organizing the mitotic spindle, a microtubule-based structure that centers and then segregates the chromosomes during cell division.
When a cell divides, it normally possesses two centrosomes, allowing the cell to build a bipolar spindle and accurately segregate the chromosomes to two daughter cells.
Appropriate control of centrosome number is crucial to maintaining genome stability.
Centrosome number is largely controlled by their regulated duplication.
The protein Plk4 (Polo-like kinase 4), which is essential for centrosome duplication, must be strictly limited because an overabundance leads to excess centrosome duplication.
Protein phosphatase 1 is a critical regulator of the Caenorhabditis elegans Plk4 homolog known as ZYG-1.
When protein phosphatase 1 is down-regulated, ZYG-1 levels increase, leading to centrosome amplification.
The identified mechanism involving protein phosphatase 1 limits centrosome duplication.

The freshwater snail Biomphalaria glabrata is an intermediate host for the parasitic flatworm Schistosoma mansoni, which causes the disease schistosomiasis that affects over 260 million people worldwide.
Studies of Biomphalaria glabrata have identified many factors, some with high homology to known immune molecules in other organisms and many more that are unique with no known homology.
Research into the functional and mechanistic roles of the factors identified in Biomphalaria glabrata has only recently progressed.
A Toll-like receptor (TLR) was identified in Biomphalaria glabrata and its functional relevance was demonstrated in this study.

Transcriptional expression of the Toll-like receptor (TLR) was rapidly induced in a Biomphalaria glabrata snail strain that is resistant to Schistosoma mansoni, in a pattern consistent with the resistant phenotype.
Knockdown of the Toll-like receptor (TLR) resulted in 43% of resistant Biomphalaria glabrata snails becoming infected with Schistosoma mansoni to patency.
