The demonstration of the functional relevance of the Toll-like receptor (TLR) in Biomphalaria glabrata advances the understanding of the mechanistic basis of snail-schistosome compatibility.
The study contributes novel functionality to Toll-like receptors (TLRs), which are one of the most evolutionarily conserved pattern-recognition receptors and cognate signalling pathways in immunity.
The planarian displays a remarkable ability to regenerate any tissue from mere fragments of its original size.
The high capacity of the planarian to regenerate is attributed to the abundant population of pluripotent adult stem cells.
In response to an injury such as an amputation, stem cells in the planarian proliferate and replace the lost tissues de novo through epimorphosis.
Existing tissue in the planarian must rescale to the correct proportions in relation to the new fragment size through morphallaxis.
The molecules that control either the responses to injury or the ones that mediate size and scaling in planarian regeneration are not well understood.
Yki, the effector of the Hippo signalling cascade, is a critical molecule that influences several injury processes during planarian regeneration.
Loss of Yki function in regenerating planarian animals resulted in increased and temporally dysregulated expression of wound-induced genes, proliferation, and apoptosis.
Genes that are injury induced were mis-expressed in planarian animals subjected to Yki RNA interference, which also showed increases in the epidermal and muscle cell populations.
The injury responses must be restricted to ensure proper regenerative outcomes of correct scale in planarian regeneration.
Yki is a key regulator of injury responses during planarian regeneration.
Two-Component Signaling (TCS) systems are a primary means by which bacteria sense their constantly changing external environment.
For pathogens, Two-Component Signaling (TCS) relays are key to the pathogens' host survival.

A typical Two-Component Signaling (TCS) pair consists of a sensor protein which, upon an environmental stimulation, initiates a cellular response by transferring a phosphate group onto a crucial aspartate amino acid within a secondary receiver (REC) protein.
Some receiver (REC) proteins are missing key amino acids involved in the Two-Component Signaling (TCS) relay process, including the aspartate residue required for the signaling relay.
On average, there are two Aspartate-Less Receiver (ALR) proteins present in every microbial species.
The Repressor of Iron Transport Regulator (RitR) from the human pathogen Streptococcus pneumoniae is a founding member of the Aspartate-Less Receiver (ALR) family.
Aspartate-Less Receiver (ALR) proteins might have evolved to accommodate more diverse environmental signals while largely retaining their ancestral post-input signaling mechanisms.
Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) is an important cause of neurologic infections in Asia, resulting in substantial disability and deaths.
Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) is believed to be endemic in the Philippines.
Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) is an important cause of encephalitis and febrile illness in all three major island groups of the Philippines.
The majority of Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) cases in the Philippines were seen in children younger than 15 years.
Males were more often affected than females by Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) in the Philippines.
The national laboratory in the Philippines initiated testing of referred cases of Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) in 2009.
Surveillance for acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) with laboratory confirmation of a subset of cases was established in the Philippines in 2011.
From 2011 to 2014, there were 1,032 cases of suspected Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) in the Philippines.
Of 497 cases with specimens tested from 2011 to 2014 in the Philippines, 73 cases (15%) had laboratory-confirmed Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV).
Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) has an extensive geographic distribution in the Philippines.
The findings of the review support the introduction of Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) vaccine into the Philippines’ routine immunization program.
Human inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a family of chronic inflammatory disorders of the gastrointestinal tract which affect genetically susceptible individuals.
Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a lifelong disease involving mostly young people, often severely.
Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis are the two major forms of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).
Although the exact cause of Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis remains unknown, both genetic and environmental factors together play significant roles in the disease pathogenesis.
Several lines of evidence implicate commensal bacteria as an important pathogenic element in clinical disease, particularly in Crohn's disease (CD).
A novel microbial gene, I2, encoded by Pseudomonas fluorescens, a gram-negative commensal, may be involved in the pathogenesis of Crohn's disease (CD).

Molecular and immunological approaches were used to identify the human receptor for the microbial antigen encoded by the I2 gene, to characterize the ligand-receptor interactions, and to determine the three-dimensional structure of the microbial gene product.

The pfiT is a T cell superantigen, which may help to explain how microbial flora can trigger immune activation in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and may provide the groundwork for novel therapies to treat Crohn's disease (CD).

The pathogenic bacterium Citrobacter rodentium naturally infects mice using a mechanism similar to those employed by certain strains of Escherichia coli that cause severe gastrointestinal infections in humans.
Citrobacter rodentium is an important model organism for human disease research.
The genome of Citrobacter rodentium strain ICC168 has many features in common with other bacterial pathogens that have recently adapted to live in a new environment and colonise new hosts.
The genome of an additional strain of Citrobacter rodentium that was independently isolated on a different continent is remarkably similar to the genome of strain ICC168.

The genome of Citrobacter rodentium is unstable and exists in multiple conformations within a single population due to genomic inversions, recombination between repetitive sequences, and horizontally acquired DNA that is mobile within the genome.
Citrobacter rodentium recently evolved to become a pathogen of mice, possibly concurrently with the development of mouse models for human diseases, and it is still adapting to its new environment.
Schistosoma mansoni is the main species causing intestinal and hepatic schistosomiasis worldwide.
Snails of the genus Biomphalaria are best known for their role as intermediate hosts of Schistosoma mansoni.

Molecular xenomonitoring for large-scale screening of snails from transmission sites to detect the presence of schistosomes is an important point to consider for snail control interventions related to schistosomiasis elimination.

The study developed a new simple rapid loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) assay to detect Schistosoma mansoni in Biomphalaria glabrata snails under different situations of infection including early prepatent period, light or low-grade infections, and in snails pooled samples.
A simple and rapid method for DNA extraction from Biomphalaria glabrata snails' tissues was successfully used in the study.
The LAMP assay named Biompha-LAMP could be potentially useful for large-scale screening to search for Biomphalaria glabrata snails infected with Schistosoma mansoni in field applicable conditions.
Modification of histone proteins is an important transcriptional regulatory mechanism in eukaryotic cells.
Various histone modifications are found primarily within the coding regions of transcribed genes.
Mono-ubiquitylation of histone H2B (H2Bub1) is needed for co-transcriptional methylation of histone H3 at specific sites.

Cdk9, the kinase component of positive transcription elongation factor b (P-TEFb), and H2Bub1 are jointly regulated by a positive feedback loop in which Cdk9 activity is needed for co-transcriptional H2Bub1.
H2Bub1 stimulates Cdk9 activity toward the conserved elongation factor Spt5.
The combined action of H2Bub1 on Spt5 phosphorylation and histone methylation accounts for the gene-regulatory effects of H2Bub1.
Positive transcription elongation factor b (P-TEFb) and H2Bub1 act in opposition on elongating RNA polymerase according to genetic and genome-wide studies.
The positive feedback linking positive transcription elongation factor b (P-TEFb) and H2Bub1 helps to maintain a balance between their opposing actions.
A conserved histone modification has a novel regulatory role during transcription elongation.
Exposure to environmental chemicals and drugs may have a negative effect on human health.
An essential step towards understanding the effect of chemicals on human health is to identify all possible molecular targets of a given chemical.
Various network-oriented chemical pharmacology approaches have been published recently.
Existing network-oriented chemical pharmacology methods limit the protein prediction to already known molecular drug targets.
New findings can be made by using high-confidence protein-protein association databases.
The described generic computational systems biology model aims to understand the underlying molecular mechanisms of chemicals and the biological pathways they perturb.
The novel and complementary approach integrates toxicogenomics data, chemical structures, protein-protein interaction data, disease information, and functional annotation of proteins.
The high confidence protein-protein association network reveals unexpected connections between chemicals and diseases or human proteins.
The authors provide literature support to demonstrate the validity of some predictions and illustrate the power of an approach that integrates toxicogenomics data with other data types.
Plant-fermenting bacteria are important for the global carbon cycle, human nutrition, and industrial production of renewable fuels and commodities from cellulosic biomass.
Plants are primarily composed of heterogeneous polysaccharides, requiring plant-degrading microbes to encode many carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) to cleave different sugar linkages.

The authors developed a broadly applicable method to study how microbes catabolize plant biomass by determining the combination of carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) that depolymerize each polysaccharide into sugars, how the cell alters global mRNA expression, and the efficiency with which each polysaccharide is metabolized.
The authors applied this method to investigate how Clostridium phytofermentans, a bacterium encoding 171 carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes), ferments polysaccharides.
The authors assimilated their results into a genetic model of how Clostridium phytofermentans metabolizes plant biomass.
The pancreas produces many different hormones, as well as several substances important for digestion.
The pancreas contains different types of cells to perform its roles, for example, acinar cells make digestive enzymes that help to break down food.
Pancreatic cells can accumulate mutations in their DNA that cause them to divide, acquire an altered identity and form a cancerous tumor.
The DNA of cells is packed into a structure called chromatin.
While the DNA sequence is essentially the same across all normal cells of a given individual, chromatin can be more or less compacted in the different cell types that comprise our body tissues.
A collection of proteins called the SWI/SNF complex can reorganize the chromatin to change how tightly the DNA is packed.
The SWI/SNF complex determines which genes in the DNA are accessible and can be activated, and which ones cannot.
Around 25% of pancreatic cancers contain mutations in genes that produce proteins of the SWI/SNF complex.
These mutations normally occur with an additional mutation that over-activates the gene that produces a potentially cancer-causing protein called Kras.

Livshits et al. genetically engineered mice to investigate how one SWI/SNF complex protein called Arid1a affects how pancreatic cancer develops by temporarily halting the production of Arid1a in acinar cells by feeding these mice an antibiotic.
The gene that produces Kras was over-activated in the pancreases of the genetically engineered mice, making them more likely to develop cancer.
Within two weeks of stopping the production of Arid1a, the acinar cells stopped producing digestive enzymes and started making other proteins that are typically found in cancerous cells.
Arid1a is involved in maintaining the normal identity and activity of pancreatic acinar cells.
Restoring the ability of altered acinar cells to produce normal levels of Arid1a by removing the mice from the antibiotic diet did not reverse the changes in protein production.
Biochemical experiments showed that acinar cells with reduced levels of Arid1a have altered chromatin.
In mice with over-active Kras and reduced levels of Arid1a, the genes that produce digestive enzymes, which are normally active in healthy pancreases, were less accessible.
The results presented by Livshits et al. provide the first evidence of how alterations to Arid1a can lead to irreversible changes in the identity and activity of pancreatic acinar cells.
Methods that attempt to restore the functions of absent SWI/SNF proteins to cancer cells are unlikely to treat the cancer successfully.
Flies and humans are descended from a common ancestor that existed over 600 million years ago.
Some differences between animal species are due to them having different genes, which are stretches of DNA that contain the instructions to make proteins and other molecules.
Differences between animal species are often caused by the same or similar genes being switched on and off at different times and in different tissues in each species.
The instructions that control when and where a gene is expressed are written in the sequence of DNA bases located in the regulatory region of the gene.
The instructions that control gene expression are written in a language often called the ‘gene regulatory code’.
Proteins called transcription factors read and interpret the gene regulatory code by binding to specific sequences of DNA, or ‘DNA words’, and increase or decrease gene expression.
Changes in gene expression between species could be due to changes in transcription factors and/or changes in the instructions within the regulatory regions of specific genes.
Gene regulatory regions are not well conserved between species.

It is unclear if the instructions in gene regulatory regions are written using the same gene regulatory code and whether transcription factors found in different species recognize different DNA words.
Nitta et al. used high-throughput methods to identify the DNA words recognized by 242 transcription factors from a fruit fly called Drosophila melanogaster.
Nitta et al. used new computational tools to find motifs, or collections of DNA words, that are recognized by each of the transcription factors.
Nitta et al. observed that, despite more than 600 million years of evolution, almost all known motifs found in humans and mice were recognized by fruit fly transcription factors.
Both fruit flies and humans have transcription factors that recognize a few unique motifs and confer properties that are specific to each species.
Some of the transcription factors that control the development of the fruit fly wing are not present in humans.
Fruit flies lack both mucus-producing goblet cells and the ability to recognize a motif read by the transcription factor that controls the development of these cells in humans.
The findings of Nitta et al. indicate that transcription factors do not evolve to recognize subtly different DNA motifs but instead appear constrained to recognize the same motifs.
The gene regulatory code that determines how DNA sequences direct gene expression is highly conserved in animals, much like the genetic code that instructs how to build proteins.
The language used to guide the development of animals has remained very similar for millions of years.
Differences between animals are due to differences in the content and length of the instructions written using the gene regulatory code into the regulatory regions of their genes.
The seeds of rice, wheat and other flowering plants store a variety of nutrients, largely in the form of sugars, proteins and oils.
The stored reserves in the seeds of rice, wheat and other flowering plants provide the main source of calories for humans and livestock all over the world.
Seed development begins after male sperm cells fuse with female gametes inside the flower.
The fusion of male sperm cells with female gametes inside the flower leads to the formation of the embryo and a structure called the endosperm.
The embryo will develop into a new plant.
The endosperm nourishes the growing embryo.
A protective seed coat surrounds the embryo and endosperm and develops from certain parts of the parent flower.
The embryo, endosperm, and seed coat have to communicate to coordinate their growth for the seed to develop successfully.
Auxin is a key plant hormone that is needed for plants to grow and develop properly and is necessary for the endosperm to form.
Previous research has shown that the endosperm is required to trigger the formation of the seed coat.
The signal that triggers the formation of the seed coat has not yet been identified.
The endosperm produces auxin, which acts as a molecular signal for the seed coat to start forming in the flowering plant Arabidopsis thaliana.
Exposing unfertilized flowers to auxin caused a seed coat to form even though the endosperm was absent.
Auxin alone is sufficient to trigger the formation of the seed coat without any other signals.
A protein called AGL62 regulates the movement of auxin to the parts of the flower that give rise to the seed coat.
In the absence of AGL62, auxin remains trapped in the endosperm and the seed coat fails to develop.
Cancer cells typically cannot spread between individuals, but there are a few examples of contagious tumours.
Two examples of contagious tumours have emerged in a single species, the Tasmanian devil, a marsupial carnivore.
The contagious tumours in Tasmanian devils are known as Devil Facial Tumour 1 (or DFT1) and Devil Facial Tumour 2 (or DFT2), and both cause tumours around the faces of infected devils.
Since it emerged in the 1990s, Devil Facial Tumour 1 (DFT1) has killed 60–90% of the Tasmanian devil population.
Preserving the few remaining healthy Tasmanian devils has been a major challenge for conservationists.
The challenge of preserving healthy Tasmanian devils became more urgent in 2014 when the second contagious cancer, Devil Facial Tumour 2 (DFT2), was discovered circulating in the population.
Contagious cancers are rare because the immune system usually eliminates cells coming from outside the body.
Each healthy cell carries molecules known as the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) that act as a barcode showing where each cell comes from.
The immune system uses the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules to help it tell the difference between the body’s own cells and those from elsewhere.
Devil Facial Tumour 1 (DFT1) can avoid the immune system and spread to new hosts because it has lost the major histocompatibility complex (MHC).
In 2014, scientists identified a new Tasmanian devil cancer named Devil Facial Tumour 2 (DFT2), but it was unclear how this second cancer evades the immune system as it spreads from host to host.
Caldwell et al. examined the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) on cells from Devil Facial Tumour 2 (DFT2) cancers, including cells grown in the laboratory and cells taken from cancer biopsies.

Biochemical tests showed that the Devil Facial Tumour 2 (DFT2) cells do carry major histocompatibility complexes (MHCs), but that the MHC barcodes of DFT2 are similar to those of the Tasmanian devils infected with the disease.

The similarity of the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) barcodes in Devil Facial Tumour 2 (DFT2) cells and infected Tasmanian devils may explain how the cancer can spread undetected in these animals because the immune system does not recognize it as coming from outside the body.
Further analyses reveal that the Devil Facial Tumour 2 (DFT2) cancer cells are slowly evolving to lose their major histocompatibility complexes (MHCs).
Devil Facial Tumour 2 (DFT2) could, with time, become as contagious as Devil Facial Tumour 1 (DFT1).
Devil Facial Tumour 1 (DFT1) and Devil Facial Tumour 2 (DFT2) threaten the future of the Tasmanian devil.
Tasmanian devils are top predators and are key to the ecosystem in Tasmania.
Preservation of Tasmanian devils is vital to the ecosystem in Tasmania.
Devil Facial Tumour 2 (DFT2) provides a unique opportunity to study an emerging cancer as it develops.
Research on Devil Facial Tumour 2 (DFT2) will help to protect Tasmanian devils and may lead to effective vaccines.
The results of the research on Devil Facial Tumour 2 (DFT2) could reveal how other cancers avoid the immune system and may help to detect them during treatment.
There are many similarities between contagious cancer cells and organ transplants.
Understanding the role of the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) in Devil Facial Tumour 2 (DFT2) could lead to better ways to prevent rejection following organ transplants.
The human body is made up of about 200 different types of cells, all of which are descended from a single fertilised egg.
As an embryo develops, its cells divide and specialise into distinct lineages.
Cells in each lineage go on to form a restricted number of cell types that are required to make a specific tissue.
During early development, cells switch from being pluripotent, with the potential to become many different cell types, to committing to one particular cell lineage.
Controlling the process of cell lineage commitment involves a huge number of signalling proteins and pathways.

Bone morphogenetic protein, or BMP, is a signalling protein that stops pluripotent cells turning into nerve tissue and encourages embryonic stem cells to contribute to the mesoderm of the early embryo.
The mesoderm of the early embryo goes on to form the muscles, connective tissues, and some blood cells.
BMP is known to trigger the production of proteins known as Id factors, which stands for inhibitor of differentiation.

Malaguti et al. investigated the roles of BMP and Id factors in controlling mouse embryo development and found that these proteins needed help from a third protein to stop pluripotent cells turning into nerve tissue.
The third protein, called E-Cadherin, normally helps cells to adhere to other cells.
Losing E-Cadherin encourages cells to become either nerve or mesoderm tissues.
A drop in E-Cadherin levels must occur before nerve tissue can form.
Encouraging cells to become part of the mesoderm requires BMP to activate another pathway that does not require E-Cadherin.
The two effects of BMP can be uncoupled by adjusting the levels of E-Cadherin.
At low concentrations, BMP can keep cells pluripotent but cannot encourage cells to commit to a mesoderm fate.
At higher doses, BMP primes cells to respond to the signals that trigger their development into mesoderm tissue.
Manipulating both E-Cadherin and BMP signalling could improve the ability to generate useful cell types, such as neurons, from stem cells grown in laboratory cultures.
The cells of nearly all organisms need iron as this metal plays an important role in a wide range of biological processes.
Iron can trigger the formation of harmful molecules that can damage cells.
The amount of iron in cells is tightly controlled and any extra iron is safely stored away.
Most of the iron in the body is stored within a protein called ferritin.
Ferritin is broken down to release iron as it is needed in a process known as ferritinophagy.
Cells use several systems to break down proteins, one of which is called autophagy and has been linked to ferritinophagy.
During autophagy, a bubble-like structure called an autophagosome engulfs proteins that need to be removed and delivers them to a compartment in the cell where they can be broken down.
In 2014, researchers showed that a protein called NCOA4 on the surface of autophagosomes targets ferritin for destruction.
When iron levels are high in the cell, the amount of NCOA4 on the autophagosomes is low.
Low amounts of NCOA4 on autophagosomes lead to fewer ferritin molecules being broken down.
Low iron levels lead to an increase of NCOA4 on autophagosomes, which promotes ferritinophagy and increases the amount of iron in the cell.
A region of NCOA4 directly interacts with a particular subunit of ferritin and this interaction is necessary to deliver ferritin to autophagosomes.
The amount of NCOA4 varies depending on whether NCOA4 interacts with another protein called HERC2, which targets proteins for destruction by a structure called the proteasome.
HERC2 only binds to NCOA4 when iron levels are high, which leads to NCOA4 being broken down by the proteasome.
When iron levels are low, HERC2 does not interact with NCOA4.
The presence of more NCOA4 leads to more ferritinophagy and increases the amount of iron in the cell.
Red blood cells, which depend highly on iron, do not develop properly in zebrafish that have lower amounts of the NCOA4 protein.
The cell relies on direct interactions among proteins and compartments called organelles to stay alive.
Manipulating interactions among proteins and organelles allows researchers to control a wide variety of cell behaviors.
A system called ‘Magnets’ uses light to trigger interactions between proteins.
The Magnets system uses a segment of a protein called Vivid from a common bread mold that responds to light.
When light shines on two Vivid protein segments, it causes them to bind together in a process known as dimerization.
In the Magnets system, Vivid segments are attached to specific proteins or organelles.
By using light, researchers can force their target molecules to come together and trigger signals that can change cell behavior in the Magnets system.
The Magnets system has limitations including stability and low efficiency that require cells to be kept at low temperatures and several copies of Vivid protein segments to be used.
The low temperature requirement and multiple copies of Vivid protein segments in the Magnets system can interfere with the activity of the target proteins.
Benedetti et al. added mutations to make the Vivid protein more similar to proteins found in fungi that thrive at temperatures around 50°C to expand the Magnets technique.
The mutations made the enhanced Magnets system capable of working at body temperature in mammals.
Further mutations at the interface between the two Vivid protein segments improved the efficiency of dimerization in the Magnets system.
The enhanced Magnets system was tested in different applications including delivering proteins to different organelles and bringing organelles together.
The enhanced Magnets system should enable researchers to control a greater variety of signaling events in the cell.
The methodology established for improving the efficiency of the Magnets system could be useful to researchers working on other proteins.
Behaviors from reading to reaching for objects require large numbers of neurons to fire at the same time.
Electrodes on the surface of the scalp or within the brain itself can detect coordinated neuronal activity in the form of brain waves or oscillations.
Different regions of the brain produce oscillations with different frequencies.
Areas that control movement, known collectively as the motor system, generate oscillations with a frequency of 25 to 40 cycles per second, called beta oscillations.
Beta oscillations emerge when individuals are paying attention, processing cues to decide where to move, or waiting to move.

Patients with Parkinson’s disease, who suffer from tremors, slowed movements, and have trouble initiating movements, show increased beta oscillations when their symptoms are worst compared to when their symptoms are well controlled.
Existing tools for activating or silencing neurons do not allow manipulation of large groups of neurons with fine enough control to study oscillations precisely.
Khanna and Carmena trained rhesus macaque monkeys to mentally control their own brain waves.
The rhesus macaque monkeys, which had electrodes implanted in their brains, learned to increase or decrease their beta oscillations on demand.
After achieving the correct level of beta oscillations, the rhesus macaque monkeys had to reach towards a target with their arm in order to obtain a reward.
Khanna and Carmena found that the rhesus macaque monkeys took longer to initiate arm reaches when they had higher levels of beta oscillations.

When the rhesus macaque monkeys increased their beta oscillations, populations of neurons exhibited patterns of activity that looked very different from the patterns occurring at the start of movement.
When neurons generate beta oscillations, the motor system is pausing at the expense of being ready to quickly start moving.
Pausing the motor system is sensible when paying close attention to a task, deciding where to move, and while waiting.
Too much pausing may slow down movements and make it difficult to initiate them, potentially explaining the link between worsened symptoms and higher beta oscillations seen in Parkinson’s disease.
The findings of Khanna and Carmena indicate that beta oscillations reflect brain states in which individuals are pausing.
Khanna and Carmena provide a new tool for studying how oscillations relate to behavior.
Almost every cell in human bodies has the same genes but at any one time different genes will be switched on in different cells.
Much of the DNA in a cell is wrapped around proteins called histones to form a compact structure called chromatin.
The DNA in chromatin is often so tightly packed that the genes in the DNA cannot to be accessed or switched on.
A complex of proteins called the Polycomb Repressive Complex 1 (PRC1) packs DNA into chromatin to switch genes off and keep them off in both plants and animals.
Other proteins are known to weakly bind to the Polycomb Repressive Complex 1 (PRC1), including one called SCM in fruit flies.
The protein SCM in fruit flies has not been extensively studied.
Bonasio, Lecona et al. have looked at a related version of the SCM protein that binds to chromatin in humans.
The protein SCML2A binds to molecules of RNA in humans.
Bonasio, Lecona et al. identified a previously unrecognized domain within SCML2A that interacts with RNA molecules.
SCML2A needs its RNA-binding region to be able to bind to chromatin in order to target and switch off certain genes.
The findings of Bonasio, Lecona et al. support models whereby RNA molecules can regulate the expression of genes.
Some RNA molecules regulate gene expression by interacting with SCML2A.
Humans, in general, are not particularly good at making economic decisions.
People can be influenced by unhelpful biases such as loss aversion, where a person views losses as more significant than gains.
Sometimes these biases stop people from making the decisions that offer the best reward.
Two regions near the front of the brain are known to be involved in human decision-making in response to rewards.
Many researchers disagree as to what the two brain regions near the front of the brain are actually doing when humans make economic decisions.

Much of the research in this area has asked participants to essentially gamble on a series of independent events, which typically provide a one-off instant reward with no further positive consequences.
These gambling tasks do not accurately reflect real economic decisions.
In real life situations, people tend to take time to make a decision and weigh up the potential long-term costs and benefits of an investment.
The decision itself may be deferred until enough information is gathered; for example, very few people would choose to buy a house on the spur of the moment.
Tsetsos et al. designed a task that encompasses many of the factors involved in real life decision-making to bridge the gap between previous studies and everyday experiences.

In the task designed by Tsetsos et al., participants were given the option of deciding whether to commit to or reject an investment opportunity immediately or to defer making the decision until later.
Using brain imaging, Tsetsos et al. found that the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dorsal ACC) was involved in weighing up the cost of rejecting an offer but not accepting it.

The rostromedial prefrontal cortex (rmPFC) was involved in assessing the value of an offer only when the participant decided to defer making a decision, and not when the participant decided to commit.

Using computer simulations with the more realistic task, Tsetsos et al. found that biases such as loss aversion were beneficial and helped participants make decisions that increased their financial payoff.
The unhelpful biases often seen in traditional decision-making tasks may result from participants' real life strategies failing to work when applied to an artificial situation.
Humans may not be so bad at economic decision-making after all.
Antibodies are proteins that stick to harmful substances, such as bacteria and other disease-causing pathogens, marking them for destruction or blocking their attack in the immune system.
Antibodies are highly selective, and this ability has been used to target particular molecules in research, diagnostics and therapies.
Typically, antibodies need to stick to a particular segment, or ‘epitope’, on the surface of a cell in order to trigger an immune response.
Knowing where epitopes are can help explain how antibodies work and aid the development of more effective drugs and diagnostic tools.
One way to identify epitopes is to measure the nano-distance between antibodies and other features on the cell surface.
Researchers take multiple images of the cell the antibody is attached to using light microscopy to measure the nano-distance between antibodies and other features on the cell surface.
Various statistical methods are applied to create an ‘average image’ with higher resolution that can be used to measure the distance between two points more accurately.
The existing approach to measuring distances works on fixed shapes like a perfect circle but cannot handle human cells and bacteria which have less uniform and more complex surfaces.
Kumra Ahnlide et al. have developed a new method called SiteLoc which can overcome the barrier of measuring distances on uneven surfaces like human cells and bacteria.
The SiteLoc method involves two fluorescent probes: one attached to a specific site on the cell’s surface, and the other attached to the antibody or another molecule of interest.
The two fluorescent probes emit different colours when imaged with a fluorescent microscope.
To cope with objects that have uneven surfaces, such as cells and bacteria, the two fluorescent signals are transformed to follow the same geometrical shape.
The relative distance between the two fluorescent probes is measured using statistical methods in the SiteLoc method.
Using the SiteLoc approach, Kumra Ahnlide et al. were able to identify epitopes on a bacterium and measure distances on the surface of human red blood cells.
The SiteLoc system could make it easier to develop antibody-based treatments and diagnostic tools.
The SiteLoc system could be beneficial to the wider research community for probing questions that require measuring nanoscale distances.
Embryos begin as a collection of similar cells, which progress in stages to form a huge variety of cell types in particular arrangements.
These patterns of cells give rise to the different tissues and organs that make up the body.
Humans have evolved unique ways to control organ development that differ from model organisms such as mice and frogs.
Investigating human embryonic development is difficult because experiments cannot be performed on human embryos and human development is hard to recreate in test tubes.
The current understanding of how developing human cells specialize and organize is incomplete.
Libby et al. have created a new system to study how different genes control cell organization using human pluripotent stem cells.
Human pluripotent stem cells are cells that have the ability to specialize into any type of cell.
Some of the human pluripotent stem cells are modified using a technique called inducible CRISPR interference, which makes it possible to reduce the activity of certain genes in these cells.
Libby et al. used inducible CRISPR interference to investigate how changes to the activity of two genes called ROCK1 and CDH1 affect how a mixed group of stem cells organized themselves.
Cells that lacked ROCK1 formed bands near the edges of the group in the mixed stem cell population.
Cells that lacked CDH1 segregated themselves from other cells, forming ‘islands’ inside the main group in the mixed stem cell population.
The human pluripotent stem cells retained their ability to specialize into any type of cell after forming these patterns.
Specific groups of human pluripotent stem cells were more likely to become certain cell types after forming these patterns.
The method developed by Libby et al. can be used to study a range of complex tissue development and cell organization processes.
The brain processes information through the activity of many different types of neurons.
A common assumption is that researchers can work out the role of each type of neuron by increasing or decreasing its activity experimentally and observing the consequences.
Advances in molecular genetic techniques such as optogenetics have made it easier to experimentally manipulate the activity of neurons.
Phillips and Hasenstaub used optogenetics to inactivate two types of neurons in an area of the mouse brain responsible for processing sound.
Inactivating each cell type produced different outcomes in the mouse brain area responsible for processing sound.
The standard way of interpreting the results of inactivating each cell type is to conclude that the neurons must therefore have different, separable roles.
Using optogenetics to increase the activity of the neurons revealed no differences in the neurons’ roles.
Using a computer model, Phillips and Hasenstaub showed that relatively small changes in factors such as the spontaneous activity of the neurons can affect the outcome of the experiments.
Under certain circumstances, the two types of neurons respond in the same way to activation and inactivation; under other circumstances, they respond differently.
The conclusions drawn about a neuron’s role can be sensitive to how the neuron was manipulated.
Opioids such as morphine or fentanyl are powerful substances used to relieve pain in medical settings.
Taken in too high a dose, opioids can depress breathing, leading to slow, shallow breaths that cannot sustain life.
In the United States, about 130 people die each day from opioid overdose.
Opioids influence the brain of animals, including humans, by attaching to proteins known as opioid receptors that are present at the surface of neurons.
Bachmutsky et al. genetically engineered mice that lack opioid receptors in specific brain regions that control breathing.
The genetically engineered mice were exposed to opioids, and their breathing was closely monitored.
Two small brain areas were responsible for breathing becoming depressed under the influence of opioids in the genetically engineered mice.
The brain region with the most critical impact on opioid-induced breathing depression is where the breathing rhythms originate.
A small group of 50 to 140 neurons in the brain region where breathing rhythms originate were used by opioids to depress breathing.
The small group of neurons used by opioids to depress breathing were not necessary for the drugs’ ability to relieve pain.
Neurons transmit information around the body in the form of electrical signals.
Electrical signals cannot cross the gaps between neurons.
To send a message to its neighbor, a neuron releases a molecule known as a neurotransmitter into the gap between the cells.
The neurotransmitter binds to proteins on the recipient neuron and triggers new electrical signals inside that cell.
When the message has been received, the neurotransmitter molecules are returned to the first neuron so that they can be reused.
This recycling of neurotransmitter molecules is particularly important in the visual system, where neurons communicate via rapid-fire signaling.
In fruit flies, light-sensitive neurons in the eye known as photoreceptors release a neurotransmitter called histamine when they detect light.
Supporting cells called laminar glia take up any leftover histamine and combine it with another molecule known as β-alanine to form a larger molecule.
The photoreceptors absorb this larger molecule and break it back down into histamine and β-alanine.
It is not clear how the β-alanine returns to the laminar glia to allow this cycle to continue.
Many molecules rely on so-called “transporter” proteins to help them move into or out of cells.
Han, Xiong et al. prepared a list of fruit fly genes that encode transporter proteins found inside the insect’s head to identify transporters that might help to move β-alanine.
Testing the resulting proteins in a cultured cell system revealed that one of them was able to transport β-alanine.
The protein named BalaT is found in another type of support cell called retinal pigment cells.
Mutant fruit flies that cannot produce BalaT are blind because their photoreceptors have problems in transmitting information to other neurons.
Han, Xiong et al. propose that BalaT transports β-alanine from photoreceptors to retinal pigment cells, which then pass β-alanine on to the laminar glia.
The human body has a limited ability to regenerate and repair itself after major injuries.
Flatworms, most notably planarians such as Schmidtea mediterranea, have exceptional regenerative abilities and can regrow large parts of their bodies.
Regrowing body parts is a complex process involving the coordinated creation of many different types of cells.
An important first step in understanding tissue regeneration is to develop a detailed catalog of cell types in that tissue.
Laser capture microdissection, or LCM, is a technology used to isolate and study subregions or even individual cells from within a tissue.
Laser capture microdissection can help to identify different cell types and to examine what makes them unique.
Laser capture microdissection can be used to create a detailed catalog of cells, their differences, and the roles they perform.
Forsthoefel et al. have used laser capture microdissection to study cells from the planarian digestive system.
The laser capture microdissection approach found 1,800 genes that have high activity in cells from the planarian gut and showed many similarities between planaria and humans.
Laser capture microdissection made it possible to study planarian gut cells in a new level of detail, revealing several hundred new genes as well as new cell types.
The study showed that regeneration and survival of cells known as goblet cells particularly depended on two genes, gli-1 and RREB2.
Irreversible gut damage in humans can result from surgeries and conditions such as acid reflux.
Other animals are able to repair and regenerate the gut more successfully than humans.
Techniques like laser capture microdissection can help researchers to understand the differences between humans and other species.
The Amazon rainforest in South America is the largest tropical forest in the world.
Rainforests play an important role in storing an element called carbon, which is a core component of all life on Earth.
Certain forms of carbon, such as the gas carbon dioxide, contribute to climate change.
Trees and other plants absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and then incorporate the carbon into carbohydrates and other biological molecules.
The Amazon rainforest alone holds around 30% of the total carbon stored in land-based ecosystems.
Humans selectively harvest certain species of tree that produce wood with commercial value from the Amazon rainforest.
Selective logging results in the loss of stored carbon from the Amazon rainforest.
The loss of stored carbon from selective logging can be compensated for in the medium to long term if the forest is left to regrow.
New trees and trees that survived the logging grow to fill the gaps left by the felled trees in the Amazon rainforest.
It is not clear how differences in the forest, environmental factors, and the degree of disturbance caused by logging affect the ability of the forest ecosystem to recover the lost carbon.
Piponiot et al. used computer modeling to analyze data from over a hundred different forest plots across the Amazon rainforest.
The models show that the forest’s ability to recover carbon after selective logging greatly differs between regions in the Amazon rainforest.

The overall amount of carbon recovered in the first ten years after selective logging is predicted to be higher in a region in the north known as the Guiana Shield than in the south of the Amazonian basin where the climate is less favorable.
The trees that survive selective logging play a key role in carbon recovery in the Amazon rainforest.
Cells have to be able to reliably destroy or remove molecules from their interior that they no longer need.
Structures called proteasomes play a central part in the process of cutting up and digesting proteins in cells.
Mammals have several different types of proteasomes, each made up of several protein subunits.
When a cell experiences inflammation, some proteasomes change some of their subunits and form an immuno-proteasome.
Immuno-proteasomes tend to break down proteins more quickly than standard proteasomes.
Liepe et al. combined experiments and mathematical modelling to construct a detailed model of proteasome activity.
The model shows that protein transport into and out of the proteasome chamber are the steps that limit how quickly proteasomes can break down proteins.
Protein transport into and out of the proteasome chamber are largely responsible for the different rates at which standard and immuno-proteasomes process proteins.
Liepe et al. confirmed the existence of regulatory sites within the proteasome and described how these sites are arranged.
Problems that alter the rate at which proteasomes break down proteins have been linked to tumors and neurological and autoimmune diseases.
Liepe et al.'s model enables the study of how proteasome activity is affected by drugs and facilitates investigation of ways to interfere with proteasome activity for therapeutic purposes.
The twinkling of the night sky is caused by imperfections in Earth's atmosphere.
Turbulence in the air distorts light as it passes through Earth's atmosphere, causing the light to bend and blur the image.
Astronomers use a technique called adaptive optics to get a clear picture of distant objects.
Deformable mirrors controlled by computers bend light back to correct distortion in adaptive optics.
Biologists are using adaptive optics to take a closer look at the blood vessels of the brain.
Functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is one of the most popular imaging techniques for measuring blood flow in the brain.
Functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can only achieve a resolution of around 1 millimetre, while the tiniest capillaries measure less than a hundredth of a millimetre across.
Tiny blood vessels in the brain can be examined surgically or by injecting dyes into the bloodstream, but these techniques carry a risk and can only be used in experimental animals.
The retina is part of the brain and its blood supply is easier to see because the eye is transparent.
Imperfections in the eye bend light and blur images of the cells, similar to how Earth's atmosphere blurs images of stars.
Adaptive optics allows it to become possible to see single red blood cells in the eye.
Combining adaptive optics with high-speed video could allow tracking of cells through the whole network of blood vessels in the eye.
Current blood flow measurement techniques either focus on very big vessels or very small ones and cannot get a complete picture of the whole interconnected system.
Joseph et al. have combined adaptive optics, ultrafast imaging, and a new algorithm to view the whole blood vessel network in the eye of a mouse.
The new method developed by Joseph et al. can automatically measure single blood cells even when they are moving at their highest possible speed.
The new method can capture the full range of retinal vessels, from the smallest capillaries to the largest arteries and veins.
By tracking millions of cells at a time, the new method can reveal how the pressure wave of the blood changes with each beat of the heart.
The slightest disruption in blood flow to the brain can cause irreversible damage.
Measuring blood flow is crucial to understanding what happens when things go wrong in the brain.
The new method is not invasive and uses safe levels of near-infrared light which the retina cannot see, making it safe to use in humans.
Joseph et al. have started their first studies in humans using the new method.
The baseline data obtained by Joseph et al. for healthy mice provides a starting point for comparison with mice with genetic mutations or disease.
If a protein does not fold into the correct shape, the protein may be unable to act correctly and can harm cells.
Cells contain biological machines that refold or break down misfolded proteins.
ATP-dependent AAA+ proteases are biological machines that refold or break down misfolded proteins.
The activity of ATP-dependent AAA+ proteases needs to be tightly controlled because breaking down the wrong proteins can harm cells.
ATP-dependent AAA+ proteases form ring-shaped assemblies that are composed of AAA+ proteins and an associated peptidase.
In bacteria, the AAA+ protein called ClpC can be crucial for resisting stress and infecting host cells.
Adapter proteins help to activate ClpC by binding to extra domains that are fused to or inserted into the ClpC protein.
The activation of ClpC by adapter proteins requires repressing elements that ensure that the activity of ClpC remains low when the adapter proteins are not present.
Carroni, Franke et al. used cryo-electron microscopy to study the structures of repressed and adapter-activated ClpC from the pathogenic bacteria Staphylococcus aureus.
In the repressed state, 10 molecules of ClpC interact to form two assemblies that interact via regions called middle domains.
The middle domains of ClpC have a coiled coil structure and they interact via their ends in a head-to-head manner.
In the repressed state, ClpC cannot interact with its partner peptidase and the shape of the assembly shields the sites where adapter proteins can bind.
The shielding of adapter protein binding sites in the repressed state renders ClpC inactive.
ClpC proteins with mutations to the middle domain that prevent the repressed state from forming remain in a constantly active state that is highly toxic to bacteria.
Bacteria are increasingly evolving to resist the effects of the antibiotics commonly used to treat infections.
AAA+ proteases have been identified as possible targets for new antibacterial drugs.
Disrupting the repressing activity of ClpC middle domains could be an effective way for new antibacterial drugs to work.
Most bacteria that live in and on the bodies of humans and other animals can offer benefits to their hosts, although a few are harmful and can cause disease.
Many bacteria, including some important human pathogens, have tails called flagella that rotate to move the bacteria inside their hosts.
The immune system can detect parts of bacterial flagella and eliminate the pathogen.
Bacterial flagella are made from filaments of proteins.
Some bacterial flagella are enclosed by a sheath that is similar to the outer membrane that encloses certain bacteria.
Some researchers have suggested that the sheath enclosing some bacterial flagella might prevent the immune system from detecting the proteins in the flagellum.
The Hawaiian bobtail squid collects bioluminescent bacteria within a so-called ‘light organ’.
The light organ of the Hawaiian bobtail squid undergoes a number of developmental changes to house the bioluminescent bacteria.
The Hawaiian bobtail squid uses the light from the bioluminescent bacteria to mask its own shadow, which helps the squid to avoid being detected by predators.
Only bacteria with working flagella were able to trigger the normal development of the Hawaiian bobtail squid’s light organ in young squid.
The rotation of sheathed flagella in bacteria led to the release of a molecule called lipopolysaccharide in the study by Brennan et al.
Lipopolysaccharide is a molecule known to activate the immune system in animals.
Lipopolysaccharide is one of the bacterial signals that the Hawaiian bobtail squid responds to.
When the flagella of other bacteria with sheaths, such as those that cause cholera, are rotating, there is an increase in the release of lipopolysaccharide.
Rotation of the flagella of bacteria without sheaths does not increase the release of lipopolysaccharide.
The sheath of bacterial flagella can alert the host that the bacteria are present, as shown by Brennan et al. in the study of interactions between the Hawaiian bobtail squid and a marine bacterium.
Animal cells produce many small proteins known as peptides that help cells to communicate with each other.
To become active, many of these peptides need to be chemically modified.
Peptidylglycine alpha-amidating monooxygenase (PAM) is the only enzyme that carries out a type of peptide modification called amidation and it is essential for animals to grow and survive.
Peptidylglycine alpha-amidating monooxygenase (PAM) was originally thought to have evolved in the nervous system of animals.

Recent studies have found that peptidylglycine alpha-amidating monooxygenase (PAM) is also present in green algae and in hair-like projections known as cilia, which are found on the surface of most animal cells.
There are two types of cilia: motile cilia beat rhythmically and are responsible for moving cells and fluids, while non-motile cilia sense the external environment and serve as signaling hubs.
The observations that peptidylglycine alpha-amidating monooxygenase (PAM) is present in cilia suggest that PAM may have other roles in cells in addition to activating peptides.
Kumar et al. investigated the role of peptidylglycine alpha-amidating monooxygenase (PAM) in green algae, flatworms, and mice.
Peptidylglycine alpha-amidating monooxygenase (PAM) is important for the formation of both motile and non-motile cilia.
Reducing the levels of peptidylglycine alpha-amidating monooxygenase (PAM) in green algae and flatworms resulted in short stubs forming on the surface of cells instead of motile cilia.
Reducing the levels of peptidylglycine alpha-amidating monooxygenase (PAM) in flatworms reduced the ability of flatworms to glide around their environment.
The cells of mutant mice lacking peptidylglycine alpha-amidating monooxygenase (PAM) produced non-motile cilia that were much shorter than those produced by normal mouse cells.
Further experiments suggest that peptidylglycine alpha-amidating monooxygenase (PAM) may be involved in the transport of certain proteins to the sites where new cilia will form.
The findings of Kumar et al. reveal a link between the peptidylglycine alpha-amidating monooxygenase (PAM) enzyme, amidation, and the assembly of cilia.
The nervous system contains billions of cells called neurons that connect to each other to form complex networks via junctions known as synapses.
Synapses form between the end of an elongated section called the axon of one neuron and the tiny projections called dendrites from the cell body of the next neuron.

Throughout the lifespan of an animal, the nervous system responds to experiences and stimuli from the environment by changing the strength of the connections at synapses, which is known as synaptic plasticity.
Long-term information about learning and memory can be stored and used to direct future responses to similar situations through synaptic plasticity.
Many proteins are involved in forming and altering synapses.
The genes that code for the proteins involved in forming and altering synapses are found in the nucleus of the neuron within the cell body.
To make new proteins, copies of genes are made using molecules called messenger RNAs (mRNAs), which then leave the nucleus and are used as templates by the machinery that assemble proteins.
Previous studies have shown that messenger RNA (mRNA) molecules are transported from the cell body to the axon and dendrites in neurons.
Kim et al. studied the movement of messenger RNA (mRNA) molecules in neurons from the sea slug Aplysia during synapse formation and synapse plasticity.
Kim et al. showed that messenger RNA (mRNA) molecules are delivered equally throughout the neuron and are not targeted to a particular synapse.
The level of protein production using messenger RNA (mRNA) molecules is much higher in places where synapses are being formed or altered in neurons.
A protein called netrin-1 promotes protein production in the dendrites of neurons at synapses where synapses are being formed or altered.
Kim et al. demonstrate that although messenger RNA (mRNA) molecules are delivered throughout the neuron, they are only used to make proteins at specific synapses.

The delivery of messenger RNA (mRNA) molecules throughout the neuron allows the entire neuron to be in a state of readiness to make new synapses or alter existing ones in response to stimuli from the environment.
Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) is the virus that causes acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS) in humans.
When human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infects a person, it targets cells of the immune system, which normally act to defend the body against infections.
As human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) spreads from one immune cell to the next, it weakens the immune system so that individuals become more vulnerable to other illnesses.
A cell infected with human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) creates new virus particles at its surface and then releases the particles so that they can infect other cells.
Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) viruses encode their genetic information as molecules of ribonucleic acid (RNA).

The host cell of human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) also makes many other ribonucleic acid (RNA) molecules that do not contain virus genes, so there must be a mechanism in place to ensure that the new virus particles only contain viral RNA.

An human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) protein called Gag is responsible for assembling new virus particles and several Gag proteins come together on the cell membrane to form a honeycomb-like structure called the immature lattice.
It is not clear how the human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) protein Gag is able to select the right ribonucleic acid (RNA) molecules.

Carlson et al. used artificial versions of the cell membrane, viral ribonucleic acid (RNA), and the human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) protein Gag to create a simple cell-free system to study how RNA is packaged into new HIV-1 particles.

The simple cell-free system created by Carlson et al. shows that all that is needed for viral ribonucleic acid (RNA) to be correctly packaged into new human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) particles is for the protein Gag to be attached to the cell membrane in such a way that the immature lattice forms correctly.
Disturbing the immature lattice by altering the human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) protein Gag can result in a drastic loss of ribonucleic acid (RNA) selectivity.

Other molecules in host cells called transfer ribonucleic acids (tRNAs) enhance the ability of the human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) protein Gag to select the ribonucleic acid (RNA) molecules that encode virus genes.
Carlson et al.'s findings reveal a link between the formation of the human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) protein Gag lattice and the packaging of virus genes into new virus particles.
Drugs that inhibit the process of human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) protein Gag lattice formation and virus gene packaging could have the potential to be used as therapies against HIV-1.

A future challenge will be to re-create the entire process of human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) assembly in a cell-free system, which would make it easier to develop new drugs that target the process.

The cerebellum, an area at the base of the brain, controls the coordinated effort of various muscles involved in keeping balance by sending messages in the form of electrical signals along cells called Purkinje neurons.
The electrical signals sent by Purkinje neurons consist of steady ‘tonic’ activity or short ‘bursts’ of activity.
Previous studies in unconscious mammals suggest that Purkinje neurons can spontaneously switch between tonic activity and short bursts of electrical signals.
It is technically challenging to record the voltage of single Purkinje neurons of conscious rodents.
Zebrafish larvae are small, transparent, and lack a skull, which makes it possible to record the activity of the cerebellum using tiny glass electrodes.
Even when zebrafish larvae are awake, the Purkinje cells produce either spontaneous bursts or tonic activity and can readily switch between the two.
The switch between tonic activity and bursts in Purkinje neurons is controlled in part by the voltage on the neurons' surface.
A positive voltage on the surface of Purkinje neurons is called the ‘up’ state, while a negative voltage is called the ‘down’ state.
Purkinje neurons in the ‘up’ state produce tonic pulses.
Purkinje neurons in the ‘down’ state produce short bursts of activity with the help of an ion channel called AMPAR (α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor).
Motor neurons in the spinal cord carry the final command from the nervous system to the muscles.
Sengupta and Thirumalai recorded the activity of motor neurons and Purkinje neurons at the same time.
Purkinje neurons receive a copy of the motor command that goes to the muscle and produce short bursts of electrical activity in response.
The production of short bursts of electrical activity by Purkinje neurons in response to the motor command requires AMPAR activity and is blocked by molecules that inhibit AMPAR.
The timing of short bursts of electrical activity in Purkinje neurons with respect to the motor command changes from one Purkinje neuron to another.
Many plants, fungi, and bacteria have evolved to produce small molecules that have powerful effects on the cells of other living organisms and can even kill those cells.
Naturally produced compounds from plants, fungi, and bacteria are often used as starting points for developing new drugs.
Cyclic peptides are a class of compounds that can be relatively easily produced in the laboratory and are able to penetrate cells.
Some cyclic peptides have proved to be useful for treating cancer and immune diseases.
Ternatin is a cyclic peptide produced by several species of fungi.
In high doses, ternatin can kill mammalian cells.
Carelli et al. searched a chemical database for cyclic peptides related to ternatin and identified several similar compounds that were reported to kill cancer cells.
Carelli et al. synthesized modified versions of ternatin inspired by the structures of cyclic peptides related to ternatin.
One modified version of ternatin synthesized by Carelli et al. was 500 times more potent than ternatin, meaning a much lower dose of the compound is still able to kill cancer cells.
Ternatin blocks the production of new proteins in cells.
Ternatin binds to a complex that includes a protein called elongation factor-1A (eEF1A).
Mutations in a particular region of elongation factor-1A (eEF1A) prevent ternatin from killing cells, suggesting a potential binding site for ternatin.
A longstanding goal in neuroscience is to work out how noise affects the accuracy, speed, and confidence of decision-making.

The theory known as bounded evidence accumulation states that the brain simultaneously accumulates evidence for each option it is considering until one option exceeds a threshold and is declared the winner.
The bounded evidence accumulation theory predicts that increasing the noisiness of the available information decreases the accuracy of decisions made in response.
The bounded evidence accumulation theory predicts that increasing the noisiness of the available information speeds up decision-making and increases confidence levels.

Zylberberg et al. tested the predictions of the bounded evidence accumulation theory experimentally by having human volunteers and monkeys perform trials deciding whether randomly moving dots moved to the left or to the right overall.
The noisiness of the dot motion could be changed between trials using a newly developed method.
The effectiveness of the method to change the noisiness of dot motion was confirmed by recording the activity of neurons in the region of the monkey brain that processes visual motion information.
After each trial, the human volunteers rated their confidence in their decision.

The monkeys indicated that they were not confident in a decision by opting for a guaranteed small reward on certain trials instead of the larger reward they received when they correctly indicated the direction of motion of the dots.
In both humans and monkeys, increasing the noisiness associated with the movement of the dots led to faster and more confident decision-making.
The results presented by Zylberberg et al. suggest that the brain does not always gauge how reliable evidence is in order to fine-tune decisions.
Neurons are cells in the nervous system that relay electrical signals around the brain and body.

When an electrical impulse travelling along one neuron reaches a junction called a synapse with a neighboring neuron, it stimulates small containers known as vesicles from the first cell to release their contents into the synapse.
The contents released from vesicles travel across the synapse to the neighboring neuron and may generate a new electrical impulse.
The number of vesicles at a synapse that are ready to be released varies from one to ten.
The more vesicles a neuron releases, the more likely the second neuron will produce an electrical signal of its own.
Not all electrical signals reaching a synapse stimulate vesicles to be released, and some signals only release a single vesicle.
Some vesicles have a higher likelihood of being released than others, but this eagerness does not always predict how many vesicles an individual synapse will actually discharge.

Vaden et al. used brain tissue from mice to test the possibility that the number of vesicles available at the synapse affects how many vesicles are released without altering their eagerness for release.
Activating an enzyme called protein kinase A increased the number of vesicles released from synapses in mice without changing how likely individual vesicles were to be released.
Inhibiting protein kinase A did not change individual vesicle’s eagerness to be released but decreased the number of vesicles that were discharged in mice brain tissue.
Protein kinase A modifies a molecule on the surface of vesicles known as synapsin, which controls the number of vesicles that are available for release.
The number of vesicles released at a synapse is controlled by two independently regulated parameters: the number of vesicles that are available and how eager individual vesicles are to be released.
The ability of neurons to communicate with each other is disrupted in autism spectrum disorders, Alzheimer’s disease, and many other diseases.
Learning how neurons communicate in healthy brains will help us understand what happens in the neurons of individuals with autism spectrum disorders, Alzheimer’s disease, and many other diseases.
Tiny movements of the body, such as those due to breathing, cause a person to sway by small amounts while standing still.
The brain makes active corrections to posture to prevent a person from falling over while standing.
Posture-correcting mechanisms oppose movements such as sway and keep a person standing upright.
To initiate movement such as crossing the road, the brain can either temporarily suppress posture-correcting mechanisms or reconfigure them to work in a different way.
Posture-correcting mechanisms rely upon sensory input from various sources, including the vestibular system of the inner ear.
The vestibular system of the inner ear tells the brain about the position and movement of the head in space and relative to gravity.
Monitoring vestibular system activity as a person starts to move can reveal what is happening to the posture-correcting mechanisms.
Tisserand et al. asked healthy volunteers to transition between standing still and walking or to shift their weight from one foot to the other.
Small non-painful electric currents were applied to the bones behind the volunteers' ears to induce small changes in vestibular system activity.
Sensors in the floor measured the forces the volunteers generated while standing or walking, revealing how they adjusted their balance.
The brain suppresses its posture-correcting mechanisms before people start or stop moving.
The findings about posture-correcting mechanisms have implications for robotics by potentially making it easier to program robots to show smooth transitions into and out of movement.
The findings about posture-correcting mechanisms are relevant to movement disorders such as Parkinson's disease.
One common symptom of Parkinson's disease is freezing of gait, in which patients suddenly feel as though their feet are glued to the ground.
Understanding how the brain controls movement transitions may reveal how symptoms such as freezing of gait arise in Parkinson's disease.
The DNA in genes encodes the basic information needed to build an organism or control its day-to-day operations.
Most cells in an organism contain the same genetic information, but different types of cell use the genetic information differently.
Many of the genes that are active in a muscle cell are different from those that are active in a skin cell.

Different patterns of gene activation largely determine a cell’s identity and are brought about by DNA-binding proteins or chemical modifications to the DNA, which are both forms of epigenetic regulation.
Cells occasionally change their identities in a process referred to as reprograming.
Reprograming allows tissues to be regenerated after wounding.
Reprograming has often been studied in isolated cells grown in a dish due to technical difficulties.
Seelk, Adrian-Kalchhauser et al. set out to understand how being surrounded by intact tissue influences reprograming.
The experiments made use of Caenorhabditis elegans worms because disturbing how this worm’s DNA is packaged can trigger its cells to undergo reprograming.
Seelk, Adrian-Kalchhauser et al. show that a signaling pathway found in many different animals enhances reprograming in Caenorhabditis elegans.
Increased signaling is linked to a major epigenetic mechanism seen in specific blood tumors.
The regulatory principles uncovered using the Caenorhabditis elegans worm model could eventually provide insights into a human disease.
A gene is a segment of DNA that usually carries the information required to build a protein, the molecules responsible for most of life’s processes.
A gene's DNA segment is organized in modules, with coding sections separated by portions of non-coding DNA known as introns.
When a gene is turned on, the gene gets faithfully copied into a molecule of pre-messenger RNA (pre-mRNA), which contains the alternating coding and non-coding modules.
Before pre-messenger RNA (pre-mRNA) can serve as a template to create a protein, the pre-mRNA must be processed and all the introns removed by a structure called the spliceosome.
If the processing of pre-messenger RNA (pre-mRNA) by the spliceosome goes wrong, inaccurate protein templates are produced that may be damaging for the cell.

Spliceosomes are precise molecular scissors that can recognize where a coding module stops and an intron starts, and then make a snip in the pre-messenger RNA (pre-mRNA) to remove the non-coding sequence.
The spliceosome is a complex molecular machine formed of numerous parts, including one known as U1 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (U1 snRNP), that must come together.
When a pre-messenger RNA (pre-mRNA) has several introns, a spliceosome assembles anew for each of the introns.
Braun et al. designed a new method that allows them to tag spliceosomes extracted from a human cell and follow the spliceosomes as they come together.
The experiments by Braun et al. show that spliceosomes working on different introns in the same pre-messenger RNA (pre-mRNA) actually help each other out.
As one spliceosome assembles, this assembly helps the spliceosome that processes the neighboring intron to get built.
The U1 small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (U1 snRNPs) processing nearby introns collaborate to promote the assembly and activity of the spliceosomes.
The teamwork of spliceosomes processing multiple introns is likely important to guarantee that multiple introns are cut out quickly and accurately.
As cells in the human body grow and divide, their DNA can experience changes or damage.
Most of the mutations in DNA are harmless or quickly fixed by the human body.
Sometimes a mutation can trigger a chain of genetic events that drives the cells to multiply uncontrollably, which leads to tumors.
Identifying driver mutations is complex but key to understanding how cancers start and can be fought.
Breast cancer is the most common type of cancer diagnosed in women worldwide.
Large studies have focused on sequencing the DNA of cancerous breast cells to try to identify the mutations that started the cancer.

In cancerous breast cells, a biological mechanism called the JNK (c-Jun N-terminal kinase) signaling pathway is often inactivated because mutations affect the molecules that take part in this process.
The proteins of the JNK signaling pathway act on each other until the last one, called JNK, gets switched on.
The JNK protein participates in a number of cellular processes such as DNA repair.
Girnius et al. addressed the question of whether mutations in the JNK signaling pathway drive cancer by inactivating the JNK pathway in the breast cells of mice.
Over the next year and a half, the JNK-deficient mice were more likely to get breast cancer than normal mice.
In breast cells, the JNK protein prevented tumors from appearing.
Once the tumors were present, the JNK protein was less effective at stopping them from growing.
The DNA of breast cancer cells with no JNK protein contained more genetic changes and mistakes.
The JNK signaling pathway helps to keep the genetic information healthy.
Normally, the JNK protein activates processes that fix DNA mutations.
Genetic changes which inactivate the JNK signaling pathway can drive the development of breast cancer.
Certain anti-cancer drugs kill cancerous cells by damaging their DNA.
Breast tumor cells with inactive JNK signaling pathways are less able to repair their genetic information.
Anti-cancer drugs that damage DNA could potentially work well on breast tumor cells with inactive JNK signaling pathways.

Living organisms need energy to stay alive, and in cells, this energy is supplied in the form of a small molecule called adenosine triphosphate, or ATP, a nucleotide that stores energy in the bonds between its three phosphate groups.
Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) is present in all living cells and is often referred to as the energy currency of the cell because it can be easily stored and transported to where it is needed.
It is unknown why cells rely so heavily on adenosine triphosphate (ATP) when a highly similar nucleotide called guanosine triphosphate, or GTP, could also act as an energy currency.
There are several examples of proteins that originally used guanosine triphosphate (GTP) and have since evolved to use adenosine triphosphate (ATP), but it is not clear why this switch occurred.
One suggestion is that adenosine triphosphate (ATP) is the more readily available nucleotide in the cell.

Updegrove, Harke et al. studied a protein that helps bacteria transition into spores, which are hardier and can survive in extreme environments until conditions become favorable for bacteria to grow again.

In modern bacteria, the protein that helps bacteria transition into spores uses adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to provide energy, but it evolved from an ancestral protein that used guanosine triphosphate (GTP) instead.
Updegrove, Harke et al. engineered the protein so that it became more similar to the ancestral protein and used guanosine triphosphate (GTP) instead of adenosine triphosphate (ATP).

When the protein was engineered to use guanosine triphosphate (GTP) instead of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the protein gained the ability to break down GTP and release energy from it, but it no longer performed its enzymatic function.

The fact that the engineered protein could break down guanosine triphosphate (GTP) and release energy but lost its enzymatic function suggests that both the energy released and the source of that energy are important for a protein’s activity.

Further analysis showed that the modern version of the protein has evolved to briefly hold on to adenosine triphosphate (ATP) after releasing its energy, which did not happen with guanosine triphosphate (GTP) in the modified protein.

Updegrove, Harke et al. discovered that the levels of guanosine triphosphate (GTP) in a bacterial cell fall as it transforms into a spore, while adenosine triphosphate (ATP) levels remain relatively high.

The finding that guanosine triphosphate (GTP) levels fall while adenosine triphosphate (ATP) levels remain relatively high as bacteria transform into spores suggests that ATP may have become the source of energy of choice because it was more available.
The findings from the study provide insights into how adenosine triphosphate (ATP) became the energy currency in cells and suggest that how ATP is bound by proteins can impact a protein’s activity.

The experiments by Updegrove, Harke et al. could help inform the development of drugs targeting proteins that bind nucleotides by showing that it may be essential to consider the entirety of the binding event and not just the release of energy.
Diseases of the heart and blood vessels are linked with high blood pressure.
The causes of most cases of high blood pressure are unknown.
High blood pressure is often accompanied by the reduced flow of blood through small vessels in the skin and other parts of the body that are a long way from the heart.
Previous research has shown that when a tissue is starved of oxygen, blood flow to that tissue will increase.
The hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) family of proteins help to increase blood flow to tissues in low-oxygen situations.
