Cowburn et al. exposed mutant mice that cannot produce certain hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) proteins specifically in the skin to low-oxygen conditions to investigate what role the skin plays in the flow of blood through small vessels.

Mice lacking either hypoxia-inducible factor-1 alpha (HIF-1α) or hypoxia-inducible factor-2 alpha (HIF-2α) in the skin have altered responses to oxygen starvation that affected their heart rate, blood pressure, skin temperature and general levels of activity.
Mice lacking specific proteins controlled by the hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) also responded in a similar way to oxygen starvation.
Cowburn et al. demonstrated that the way normal healthy mice respond to oxygen starvation is more complex than previously thought.
Blood pressure and heart rate rise during the first ten minutes of exposure to low oxygen levels in normal healthy mice.
Blood pressure and heart rate decrease below normal levels for up to 36 hours following the initial rise during exposure to low oxygen levels in normal healthy mice.
By around 48 hours after exposure to low levels of oxygen, blood pressure and heart rate recover, returning to normal levels in normal healthy mice.

Loss of the hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) proteins or other proteins involved in the response to oxygen starvation specifically in the skin affect when the process of blood pressure and heart rate changes starts and how long it takes.
The responses of the skin to environmental challenges may have substantial effects on how the heart pumps blood around the body.
All animals with flapping wings make sounds such as whooshing, buzzing, or whining during flight.
The hummingbird makes a distinctive humming sound that is considered more delightful than other wing sounds.
Bird wings generate large vortices of air to boost their lift and hover in the air that can generate tones.
The airflow over bird wings can be highly turbulent, which can generate loud sounds similar to the jets of air coming out of aircraft engines.
It is difficult to determine why some wings buzz whereas others whoosh or hum given the multiple sound-generating mechanisms of animal wings.
Hightower, Wijnings et al. hypothesized that the aerodynamic forces generated by animal wings are the main source of their characteristic wing sounds.
Hummingbird wings have the most features in common with different animals’ wings while also featuring acoustically complex feathers.
Hummingbird wings are ideal models for deciphering how birds, bats, and insects make wing sounds.
Hightower, Wijnings et al. studied how a species of hummingbird called Anna’s hummingbird hums while drinking nectar from a flower.
A three-dimensional acoustic hologram was generated using 2,176 microphones to measure the humming sound from all directions around Anna’s hummingbird.
In a follow-up experiment, the aerodynamic forces generated by Anna’s hummingbird wings to hover were measured.
The wingbeat of Anna’s hummingbird was filmed simultaneously in slow-motion in both the acoustic and aerodynamic experiments.

Hightower, Wijnings et al. used a mathematical model governing the wing’s aeroacoustics to confirm that the aerodynamic forces generated by hummingbird wings cause the humming sound heard when they hover in front of a flower.
The mathematical model shows that the oscillating aerodynamic forces generate harmonics, which give the hummingbird wings’ hum the acoustic quality of a musical instrument.

Using the mathematical model, Hightower, Wijnings et al. found that differences in the aerodynamic forces generated by bird and insect wings cause the characteristic timbres of their whines, buzzes, hums, or whooshes.
Hightower, Wijnings et al. determined how wing sounds scale with body mass and flapping frequency across 170 insect species and 80 bird species.
Mosquitos are unusually loud for their body size due to the unusual unsteadiness of the aerodynamic forces they generate in flight.
The results explain why larger birds are quieter and mosquitos are louder in terms of their wing sounds.
Better understanding of how the complex forces generated by animal wings create sound can advance the study of how animals change their wingbeat to communicate.

The mathematical model that explains how complex aerodynamic forces cause sound can help make the sounds of aerial robots, drones, and fans not only more silent but perhaps more pleasing, like the hum of a hummingbird.
Proteins called G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are found on the surface of cells throughout the body.
Hormones or other signal molecules, collectively known as ligands, from outside the cell can bind to G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) to activate them.
Binding of ligands to G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) causes a change in the structure of the receptor, which triggers a signal inside the cell to alter the cell’s behavior.
G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are known to form clusters of two or more receptor units.
Many drugs can bind to G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) and most of these drugs block the activity of the receptors by taking the place of the natural ligand.
Allosteric drugs bind to different sites on G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) than the natural ligands do and can inhibit or enhance binding of the ligands by altering the shape of the receptor.
Shivnaraine et al. investigated how a type of G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) called muscarinic cholinergic receptors interact within clusters.
Shivnaraine et al. developed a method to track muscarinic cholinergic receptors in mammalian cells using a fluorescent sensor that detects changes in the allosteric site.

Experiments by Shivnaraine et al. show that two or more G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) need to interact for the receptors to respond to allosteric drugs in a manner that reflects the normal effect of the drugs on the body.

The finding that two or more G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) need to interact to respond to allosteric drugs is unexpected in light of the assumption that individual receptor molecules act independently.
Shivnaraine et al.'s findings indicate that clusters of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) may play a role in the normal behavior of GPCRs in cells.
Communication in the human body runs on electricity.
Between the exterior and interior of every living cell, there is a difference in electrical charge, or voltage.
Rapid changes in membrane potential activate vital biological processes, ranging from muscle contraction to communication between nerve cells.
Ion channels are cellular structures that maintain membrane potential and help excitable cells like nerve and muscle cells produce electrical impulses.
Ion channels are specialized proteins that form highly specific conduction pores in the cell surface.
When open, ion channels let charged particles such as calcium ions through, rapidly altering the electrical potential between the inside and outside of the cell.
Most ion channels open in response to specific stimuli, a process known as gating.
Voltage-gated calcium channels contain charge-sensing domains that change shape and allow the channel to open once the membrane potential reaches a certain threshold.
Voltage-gated calcium channels play important roles in many tissues and, when mutated, can cause severe brain or muscle disease.
Different family members of voltage-gated calcium channels open at different voltage levels and at different speeds.
The first of the four voltage sensors of the studied mammalian voltage-gated calcium channel CaV1.1 controlled opening speed.

The opening speed controlled by the first voltage sensor was driven by shifts in its configuration that caused oppositely charged parts of the protein to sequentially form and break molecular bonds, a process that takes time.

The fourth voltage sensor of the studied mammalian voltage-gated calcium channel CaV1.1 set the voltage threshold at which the channel opened and did not form sequential molecular bonds, reacting fast accordingly.
Experimental tests in muscle cells engineered to produce channels with mutations in the voltage sensors confirmed the results of the computer modelling experiments.
Fernández-Quintero, El Ghaleb et al. created a dynamic computer simulation showing the detailed structure of a mammalian voltage-gated calcium channel called CaV1.1.
The computer simulation was used to predict the movements of the voltage sensing regions while the mammalian voltage-gated calcium channel CaV1.1 opened.
Parasitic worms known as helminths represent an important health problem in large parts of Africa, South America, and Asia.
Once helminth larvae enter the body, they head to the gut where they mature into adults and start laying eggs.
In areas with poor sanitation, helminth eggs may then get passed on to other individuals.
The immune system sends large numbers of immune cells to the gut to defend the body against helminths, but it usually struggles to eliminate the parasites.
Without deworming medication, helminth infection can last for many years.
Scientists study helminth infections in the laboratory by using worms that naturally infect mice.
Understanding exactly how the immune system responds to helminth infection is essential to grasp why the immune system fails to clear the worms.
It is difficult to extract immune cells from an infected gut because helminth infection creates strong local responses such as intense slime production to try to flush out the worms.

The standard procedure to obtain immune cells from the gut consists of three steps: collecting a gut segment and washing it, stripping away the surface layers with chemicals, and using enzymes to digest the tissues which are then filtered to obtain individual cells.
The standard protocol to extract immune cells from the gut is not able to extract cells during helminth infection.
Ferrer-Font et al. methodically refined every step of the immune cell extraction method and succeeded in obtaining millions of immune cells from infected guts.
For the first time, immune cells obtained from infected guts could be studied and identified using a new technology called spectral flow cytometry.

Over 40 immune cell types were followed throughout the course of helminth infection, revealing that many first responder immune cells were recruited to the gut early on when the worms were still larvae.
The first responder immune cells disappeared once the helminth worms developed into adults.
Microscopy confirmed that the first responder immune cells were found around the developing larvae, likely attacking them.
When the adult helminth worms developed, the first responder immune cells were replaced by other immune cells, which also decreased the longer the worms were present in the gut.
The new immune cell extraction process established by Ferrer-Font et al. can be paired with other technologies that reveal which genes are turned on in individual cells.
The new immune cell extraction method could help map out exactly how the body fights helminth infections and how to improve this response.
The immune cell extraction method could also be useful to extract immune cells from the gut in other challenging scenarios such as food allergies or inflammatory bowel disorders.
Many genes carry information for making proteins.
To make a protein, a working copy of the information stored in DNA is first copied into a molecule of messenger RNA.
Messenger RNA messages are then interpreted by the ribosome, the molecular machine that makes proteins.
Many messenger RNA messages are produced from each gene, and each message can be read multiple times.
The number of proteins produced cannot be completely predicted from knowing the number of messenger RNAs in cells.
Cells control how much of a given protein they produce through interactions between the messenger RNAs and other regulatory RNAs.
Regulatory RNAs bind directly to a messenger RNA message and impede protein production.
Because there are millions of RNAs in a cell, interactions between messenger RNAs and other RNAs have evolved to be highly specific.
Messenger RNAs can encounter other RNAs that could short-circuit gene regulation and lead to less protein being produced.
Umu et al. asked if short-circuit events between messenger RNAs and other RNAs are selected against during evolution.
Computational tools were used to predict the strength of binding between the RNAs found in the dominant forms of microbial life on Earth: the bacteria and the archaea.
The majority of messenger RNAs bind more weakly to the most common RNA molecules found in cells than would be expected by chance.

Weakened binding between messenger RNAs and other RNA molecules should prevent the RNA molecules from becoming tangled with each other and ensure that protein levels are not perturbed by unintended interactions between highly expressed messages and other RNAs.

Umu et al. generated versions of the gene for a green fluorescent protein that differed only in how well their messenger RNAs could avoid interacting with the most abundant RNAs in Escherichia coli cells.
Messenger RNAs designed to avoid interacting with other RNAs yielded far more protein than those that were not designed to avoid such interactions in Escherichia coli cells.
Taking RNA interaction avoidance into account can improve predictions about how much protein will be produced and should make it easier to control protein production in experimental systems.
The messenger RNAs of some bacteria do not show clear avoidance of interactions with other RNAs.
Some bacteria that do not show clear messenger RNA avoidance have a more complex internal cell structure.
More complex cells, such as those of animals and plants, which contain much larger numbers of RNAs, may use alternative means for avoiding short-circuiting events between RNAs.
Plants, animals, and fungi store much of their DNA tightly packed with proteins in a form named heterochromatin.
The arrangement of DNA as heterochromatin helps to inactivate genes that are not needed in specific cells or at specific times.
The arrangement of DNA as heterochromatin provides a way to protect the genetic material from damage.
Heterochromatin tends to form when an enzyme called a lysine methyltransferase chemically modifies some of the proteins associated with the DNA, which are known as histones.
The lysine methyltransferase enzyme modifies only some of the histones to get the process of heterochromatin formation started.
A second protein binds to the modified histones and causes more of the DNA to become packaged up as heterochromatin.
In 2012, researchers reported that the version of the lysine methyltransferase enzyme from yeast binds to RNA molecules via a portion known as its chromodomain.
The lysine methyltransferase enzyme from yeast needed to bind to RNA to help heterochromatin to form.
A similar mechanism of lysine methyltransferase enzyme binding to RNA via its chromodomain also occurs in fruit flies.
It was not clear if the lysine methyltransferase enzyme binding to RNA via its chromodomain happened in mammals like mice and humans before the new study.
The corresponding lysine methyltransferase enzyme from mice can also bind to RNA molecules via its chromodomain.
The RNA-binding activity of the lysine methyltransferase enzyme from mice was closely linked with the enzyme’s ability to target the correct histones and efficiently form heterochromatin.
The first experiments on the lysine methyltransferase enzyme’s RNA-binding activity were conducted using purified enzymes in the laboratory.
Follow-up experiments looked at the lysine methyltransferase enzyme’s activity within mouse cells.
Mutant mice lacking the lysine methyltransferase enzyme have defective heterochromatin.
Mutant mice lacking the lysine methyltransferase enzyme tend to die young.
Mutant mice lacking the lysine methyltransferase enzyme have genetic instabilities that are associated with an increased risk of tumors and male infertility.
The mechanism behind the establishment of heterochromatin has most likely been conserved over a billion years of evolution, which is when yeast and mammals last shared a common ancestor.
Specialized beta cells in the pancreas fine-tune the amount of sugar in human blood by releasing a hormone called insulin.
Beta cells produce insulin by first building an early version of the molecule called proinsulin inside a cellular compartment called the endoplasmic reticulum.
The process of producing proinsulin involves the formation of internal staples that keep the proinsulin molecule folded correctly.
Individuals developing type 2 diabetes have spikes of sugar in their blood, and their bodies often respond by trying to make large amounts of insulin.
After a while, beta cells can fail to keep up with insulin production, which brings on full-blown type 2 diabetes.
Early in type 2 diabetes, the endoplasmic reticulum of beta cells can already show signs of stress.
The exact causes of early damage to the endoplasmic reticulum in beta cells during type 2 diabetes are still unknown.

Biochemical experiments showed that even healthy beta cells contain some misfolded proinsulin molecules where the molecular staples that should fold proinsulin internally abnormally link proinsulin molecules together.
Misfolded proinsulin accumulates inside the endoplasmic reticulum of beta cells.
Obese mice in the earliest stages of type 2 diabetes have the highest levels of abnormal proinsulin in their beta cells.
Large amounts of proinsulin molecules stapling themselves to each other in the endoplasmic reticulum of beta cells could be an early hallmark of type 2 diabetes and could worsen the disease.
A protein that limits the misfolding of proinsulin is key to maintaining successful insulin production in animals eating a Western-style, high fat diet.
Hundreds of millions of people around the world have type 2 diabetes, and this number is rising quickly.
Garden dormice are small rodents which are common in European woodlands.
Garden dormice were historically widespread from Portugal in the west to the Urals (Russia) in the east.
Garden dormice are now largely confined to western Europe with north-eastern and eastern populations having become scattered and fragmented.
During the course of a year in northern and central Europe, garden dormice make the most of the warm season to fatten up and to produce up to two litters of youngsters.
When winter comes, garden dormice enter hibernation, sometimes for more than six months.
During hibernation, garden dormice must rely on their fat reserves to survive.
Every year, the young from the second litter of garden dormice have less time to prepare for the winter compared to their siblings born earlier in the season.
The late-born garden dormice individuals developed nearly twice as fast as the ones born early in the season in this study.
Both early-born and late-born garden dormice reached a similar body size, but the second-litter dormice had less fat reserves.
Just before their first winter, both early-born and late-born garden dormice increasingly started to enter torpor, which are short and daily resting-like periods when the body slows down.
Torpor rarely happens when animals are growing because growth requires a warm body, but torpor is useful to help store and consolidate fat before the cold months.
Late-born garden dormice experienced more torpor on average than their first-litter peers.
Both early-born and late-born garden dormice groups survived their first hibernation.
When garden dormice emerged from their first hibernation, late-born individuals were more likely to reproduce that year than early-born individuals.
Garden dormice which grew quickly might also have sexually matured earlier.
Animals born later in the season have a faster life history: they grow rapidly, reproduce quickly but may die younger than their early-born peers.
Early-life events can shape the course of animals’ existences and influence how their bodies operate.
The outer layer of the mammalian brain, the cerebral cortex, plays a key role in memory, attention, awareness, and thought.
Rodents have a smooth cortical surface, while the cortex of larger mammals such as primates is organized into folds and furrows.
The folds in the cortex increase the amount of cortex that can fit inside the confines of the skull and are thought to have allowed the evolution of more advanced thought processes.
Mutations in various genes are likely to have contributed to the expansion and folding of the cortex.
These mutations may not always have involved changes in the instructions encoded within the genes, but might instead have involved changes in the number of copies of a gene.
The TBC1D3 gene is only found in the great apes and is active in the cortex.
The chimpanzee genome contains a single copy of the TBC1D3 gene, whereas the human genome contains multiple copies.
Introducing the TBC1D3 gene into mouse embryos triggers changes in the embryonic cortex.
The TBC1D3 gene increases the number of a type of cell called the outer radial glial cell in the cortex in mouse embryos.
Outer radial glial cells give rise to new neurons and are usually rare in mice but abundant in the brains of animals with a folded cortex.
Experiments using samples of human brain tissue confirmed that the TBC1D3 gene is required for the outer radial glial cells to form.
The human brain tissue samples were collected from miscarried fetuses with the informed consent of the patients and following approved protocols and ethical guidelines.
Introducing the TBC1D3 gene into the mouse genome gave rise to animals with a folded cortex, rather than their usual smooth brain surface.
Genes are sections of DNA that encode the instructions to make proteins.
When a gene is switched on, the section of DNA is copied to make molecules of messenger ribonucleic acid (RNA) in a process called transcription.
Messenger RNAs are then used as templates for protein production.
In animals, plants and other eukaryotic organisms, an enzyme called RNA polymerase II is responsible for making messenger RNA molecules during transcription.
RNA polymerase II is made up of several proteins, the largest of which contains a long tail called the carboxy-terminal domain.
The carboxy-terminal domain is crucial for transcription because it serves as a landing platform for other enzymes that help to make the RNA molecules.
The carboxy-terminal domain contains multiple repeats of a string of seven amino acids, which are the building blocks of proteins.
Normally, each repeat contains three amino acids called serines.
In humans and other mammals, one of these serines is often substituted with another amino acid called lysine.
This lysine, referred to as Lysine-7, was known to be modified by the addition of a chemical group called an 'acetyl' tag.
Dias, Rito, Torlai Triglia et al. carried out an in-depth study into how Lysine-7 is modified in mouse cells and what effects these modifications have on transcription.
The experiments show that Lysine-7 can also be modified by the addition of a different chemical group called a 'methyl' tag.
This methyl modification of Lysine-7 is also found in flies, worms and human cells, which suggests that it is generally important for transcription.
In mouse stem cells, methyl tags are added to Lysine-7 during the earliest steps of transcription, before the acetyl tags are added.
A balance between the addition of methyl tags and acetyl tags to Lysine-7 fine-tunes the activity of RNA polymerase II.
These findings add to the understanding of how cells control the activity of RNA polymerase II at different genes.
The outer membrane of a cell is a tight but elastic barrier that controls what enters or leaves the cell.
Large molecules typically cannot cross the outer membrane of a cell unaided.
Large molecules must be packaged into a pocket of the membrane that is then pulled inside to enter the cell.
Endocytosis is the process that shuttles material into a cell hundreds of times a minute.
Endocytosis relies on molecular machines that assemble and disassemble at the membrane as required.
Actin is a protein that self-assembles near the membrane into long filaments with many repeated subunits during endocytosis.
Actin filaments grow against the membrane, pulling it inwards during endocytosis.
It was not clear how actin filaments organize to pull on the membrane with enough force and without a template to follow.
Akamatsu et al. used computer simulations informed by measurements made in living cells to identify how actin operates during endocytosis.
The simulations included information about the location of actin and other essential molecules, along with details of how these molecules work individually and together.
Akamatsu et al. developed a method to count the numbers of molecules of a key protein at individual sites of endocytosis.
High-resolution imaging was used to create 3D pictures of actin and endocytosis in action in human cells grown in the laboratory.
The arrangement of actin filaments depends on the starting positions of a few key molecules that connect to actin.
Imaging confirmed that flexible actin filaments bend to store energy and then release it to pull the membrane inwards during endocytosis, similar to a pole-vaulting pole.
Simulations predicted that the collection of actin filaments adapts its shape and size in response to the resistance of the elastic membrane.
The adaptation of actin filaments to membrane resistance makes the endocytosis system opportunistic and adaptable to the unpredictable environment within cells.
Spatial disorientation happens to people with damage to a brain region called the retrosplenial cortex.
The retrosplenial cortex contains ‘low-rheobase’ neurons which are not seen anywhere else in the brain.
Experiments were conducted in mice using optogenetics, a technique that activates neurons using pulses of light.

Brain areas involved in processing information about direction and position preferentially communicate with low-rheobase neurons rather than with nearby, more standard neurons in the retrosplenial cortex in mice.
Low-rheobase neurons in the retrosplenial cortex can calculate how fast a mouse is turning its head using only information about which direction the mouse is facing.
Low-rheobase neurons in the retrosplenial cortex can turn directional compass-like signals into a gyroscope signal that can track both direction and speed of head movement.
Low-rheobase neurons in the retrosplenial cortex may have evolved specifically to support spatial navigation by combining information about direction and space.
Individuals with Alzheimer’s disease show the same type of spatial disorientation as individuals with direct damage to the retrosplenial cortex.
The retrosplenial cortex is one of the first brain regions to show altered activity in Alzheimer’s disease.
In dry caves of southeastern Brazil, a group of insects named Neotrogla have egg-producing females with penises and sperm-producing males with vaginas.
The sex roles of Neotrogla Brazilian cave insects are reversed, with females competing over males and males being selective of their female partners.
The sex role reversal in Neotrogla likely evolved because the males’ semen represents a rich and reliable source of energy within a nutrient-poor cave environment.
When Neotrogla females are not using semen to fertilize their eggs, they consume the semen.
Neotrogla species alone have reversed sexual organs among animals that show sex role reversal.
Neotrogla penises are spiky and may have evolved so that females can anchor themselves to males and then mate for prolonged periods.
Prolonged mating in Neotrogla would allow females to stock up on the nutritious semen.
Compared to their closest relatives, Neotrogla species can hold twice as much semen within their sperm storage organs.

Scientists have speculated that a valve-like structure within the sperm storage organ of Neotrogla females enables extra semen storage by allowing the female to redirect semen into two separate chambers.
The small size of the sperm storage organ in Neotrogla has made it difficult to determine its inner workings.
Scientists have yet to discover a switching valve that serves the purpose of redirecting semen within the animal kingdom outside of Neotrogla.
Yoshizawa et al. examined three Neotrogla species using advanced imaging technology and detected the first example of a biological switching valve.
Neotrogla females can control the biological switching valve to switch the flow of semen between two slots.
Neotrogla females can store two batches of semen at once by using the biological switching valve.
The spiky penises of Neotrogla females help them restrain males until they have received multiple semen injections.
Yoshizawa et al. suggest that the emergence of the biological switching valve within the sperm storage organ may have promoted the evolution of the female penis in Neotrogla.
The unique switching valve of female Neotrogla may inspire new man-made machinery that could advance a range of industries.
Cats have an innate grooming behavior that follows a particular sequence as the cat methodically cleans its body parts one-by-one.
Many animals, including insects such as fruit flies, have grooming habits.
Grooming sequences are seen across different species, which suggests that grooming behavior is important for survival.
The brain organization of grooming sequences or other behaviors involving a sequence of tasks is not well understood.
Fruit flies are a good model for studying grooming behavior because they are fastidious cleaners that carry out a series of cleaning tasks to clean each body part when coated with dust.
Researchers have many genetic tools and techniques to manipulate fruit flies' behaviors.
One technique allows specific brain cells in fruit flies to be targeted and activated to trigger particular behaviors.
Dust-covered fruit flies follow a predictable sequence of cleaning tasks: they begin by using their front legs to clean their eyes, then clean their antennae and head.
Cleaning the eyes, antennae, and head likely helps to protect the sensory organs of fruit flies.
After cleaning the head, fruit flies move on to clean the abdomen, possibly to ensure that dust does not interfere with their ability to breathe.
Fruit flies clean their wings and thorax last in the grooming sequence.
Fruit flies periodically stop to rub their legs together to remove any accumulated dust before resuming the cleaning sequence.

Seeds et al. activated different sets of brain cells one-by-one in fruit flies and found that individual cleaning tasks could be triggered in the absence of dust by stimulating a specific group of brain cells.
Each cleaning task in fruit flies is a discrete behavior controlled by a subset of brain cells.
Stimulating wing-cleaning brain cells in fruit flies suppressed thorax-cleaning behavior.
Stimulating abdomen-cleaning brain cells in fruit flies suppressed wing-cleaning and thorax-cleaning behaviors.
Stimulating head-cleaning brain cells in fruit flies suppressed wing-cleaning, thorax-cleaning, and abdomen-cleaning behaviors.
A hierarchy exists in the fruit fly brain that exactly matches the sequence that fruit flies normally follow as they clean their body parts.

The findings of Seeds et al. about how the fruit fly brain coordinates grooming sequences may provide insights into other behaviors that involve a sequence of tasks, such as nest building in animals or typing in humans.
A cell can communicate with its neighbors by producing a signal, also known as a morphogen, which tells the receiving cells what to do.
Once outside the cell, a morphogen spreads through the surrounding tissue and forms a gradient with more of the molecule closer to the signaling cells and less further away.
The cells that receive the message respond differently depending on how much morphogen they get and on where they are placed in the embryo.
Some morphogens travel through long, thin cellular extensions known as cytonemes.
Cytonemes directly connect the cells that produce a morphogen with the ones that receive the molecule.
Du et al. followed a morphogen called Branchless as it traveled through fruit fly embryos to understand how cytonemes help to form gradients.
Branchless is important for sculpting the embryonic airway tissue into a delicate network of branched tubes which supply oxygen to the cells of an adult fly.
It was assumed that Branchless would diffuse passively to reach airway cells, but experiments by Du et al. showed this was not the case.
Insects were genetically engineered to produce Branchless molecules attached to a fluorescent tag to directly observe how Branchless moves among cells.

Microscopy experiments using genetically engineered fruit flies revealed that Branchless did not diffuse passively; instead, airway cells used cytonemes to reach towards the cells that produced Branchless, collecting the signal directly from its source.
The gradient of Branchless was created because airway cells near the cells that make Branchless had more cytonemes and therefore received more of the molecule compared to cells placed further away.
Genetic analysis of the airway tissue showed that Branchless acts as a morphogen to switch on different genes in the receiving cells placed in different locations.
The target genes activated by the Branchless gradient instruct the receiving cells on how many cytonemes need to be extended, which helps the gradient to maintain itself over time.
Du et al. demonstrate for the first time how cytonemes can relay a signal to establish a gradient in a developing tissue.
Proteins are strings of amino acids that have folded into a specific three-dimensional shape.
Proteins must have the correct shape to function properly, as proteins often work by binding to other proteins or molecules much like a key fitting into a lock.
Two or more proteins can bind together and form a complex to perform various tasks.
Ovchinnikov, Kamisetty, and Baker have developed a method for predicting which parts of the proteins make contact with each other in a two-protein complex.
Different species can have copies of the same proteins, but a copy from one species might have different amino acids at certain positions when compared to a related copy from another species.
When pairs of interacting proteins from different species are compared, there will be many positions in the two proteins that vary.

If the amino acid at a position in one protein varies, and the amino acid at a position in the other protein also varies such that for any given amino acid at the second position there is often a specific amino acid at the first position, these two positions are said to co-vary.
When a pair of amino acids, one from each protein in a two-protein complex, co-varied, these two amino acids tended to make contact with each other at the protein–protein interface.
Ovchinnikov et al. used the new method to make predictions about the protein–protein interfaces in 28 protein complexes found in bacteria.
Ovchinnikov et al. used the new method to make a prediction about the interface between protein subunits in the bacterial ribosome.

When the predictions made by Ovchinnikov et al. about protein–protein interfaces were checked against the actual structures, which were all known beforehand, the predictions were found to be accurate if the number of copies of each protein being compared is greater than the average length of the two proteins.
Ovchinnikov et al. predicted the amino acids on the protein–protein interfaces for another 36 bacterial protein complexes with unknown structures.
Ovchinnikov et al. presented models for four larger bacterial protein complexes.
The number of related copies for eukaryotic proteins tends to be smaller than for bacterial proteins.
There are fewer proteins to compare for eukaryotic proteins, making it harder to detect covariation when it occurs.
Certain animal species can sense the Earth’s magnetic field for the purposes of navigation.
One technological goal is to genetically engineer specific cells in the brain or elsewhere so their activity can be controlled using an external magnet.
The dream of controlling cell activity using an external magnet has been called magnetogenetics.
Recent reports claimed to have solved both the scientific and technological challenges of magnetogenetics by discovering or engineering protein molecules that are sensitive to magnetic fields.
Markus Meister calculated how strongly the proteins in the recent magnetogenetics reports would link magnetic fields to cellular activity.
The predicted effects of the proteins linking magnetic fields to cellular activity are too weak to account for the reported measurements by between five and ten orders of magnitude.
None of the recent reports have hit on a solution to magnetogenetics.
All of the proposed proteins in the magnetogenetics reports use iron atoms to couple to the magnetic field.
The proteins proposed for magnetogenetics contain far too few iron atoms to explain the reported magnetic effects.
The magnetism of small clusters of atoms is exceedingly well understood due to technological interest in making tiny magnets for data storage drives inside computers.
If any of the biological reports of magnetogenetics were correct, they would force a revolutionary rethinking of basic physics.
In the earliest stages of development, animal cells undergo multiple rounds of division without growth via a process known as mitosis.
Over the course of just 12 rounds of cell division, a single fertilized egg is transformed into more than 4000 smaller cells.
Before dividing, the cell must first replicate its chromosomes.
A structure called the mitotic spindle separates the members of each chromosome pair and distributes them evenly between the two daughter cells.
Given that the daughter cells become smaller with each round of division, the mitotic spindle must also become smaller to ensure that the chromosomes are pulled apart an appropriate distance.

Wilbur and Heald reported insights into the mechanism by which mitotic spindle size is coordinated with cell size using the model organism Xenopus laevis, a frog that produces large embryos that are easy to manipulate.

Wilbur and Heald prepared extracts of cytoplasm from Xenopus laevis embryos at two different developmental stages: one set of embryos contained 4 cells each and the other set contained approximately 4000 cells.

The mitotic spindle, which is composed largely of microtubules—hollow filaments that can become longer or shorter through the addition or removal of tubulin building blocks—was almost twice as large in the four-cell Xenopus laevis embryos as in the more developed embryos containing approximately 4000 cells.
Mitotic spindle size was determined by the actions of two proteins: kif2a and importin-α.
Binding of kif2a destabilized microtubules and caused them to shorten.
Importin-α blocked the destabilization of microtubules by binding to kif2a and preventing kif2a from interacting with microtubules.
Wilbur and Heald found that over the course of development, importin-α became increasingly localized to the cell membrane, resulting in less importin-α available to bind to kif2a in the cytoplasm.
The reduction in cytoplasmic importin-α freed up kif2a to interact with and destabilize microtubules, leading ultimately to a reduction in mitotic spindle size.
The overall ratio of cell surface membrane to cytoplasm increases as cells undergo division without growth.
Interaction between kif2a and importin-α could be the mechanism by which mitotic spindle size and cell size are coordinated early in development.
Transposable elements are sequences of DNA that can move between different locations within a genome and are often referred to as ‘jumping genes’.
Transposable elements are found in many organisms and can make up almost 50% of the DNA in the human genome.
Transposable elements are grouped by how they move to new locations in a genome.
Some transposable elements move by a cut-and-paste mechanism whereby the transposable element DNA is removed from one location and inserted back at a new genomic location.

Retrotransposons are transposable elements that move by a copy-and-paste mechanism in which the DNA sequence is transcribed into an RNA intermediate and then copied back into DNA before being inserted into a new location.
Retrotransposons can accumulate to great numbers in genomes, and the retrotransposon called LINE-1 is present at an estimated 500,000 copies in the human genome.
Although most copies of LINE-1 are inactive, the average human genome contains about 80–100 copies that are predicted to be able to ‘jump’ to new locations.
The enzyme APOBEC3A is known to limit the movement of LINE-1 retrotransposons in cells.
APOBEC3A can alter the letters, or bases, that make up the genetic code by acting on single-strand DNA to change cytosine bases to uracil bases.
No evidence for mutation of LINE-1 sequences by APOBEC3A had been found before the study by Richardson et al.
Richardson et al. recreated the copying of LINE-1 RNA back into DNA in a test tube and revealed that APOBEC3A can mutate single-strand LINE-1 DNA.
As long as the RNA intermediate and DNA copy remain together, the LINE-1 DNA is protected from mutation by APOBEC3A.
When LINE-1 inserts into a new location, the temporarily exposed single strand of LINE-1 DNA becomes susceptible to mutation by APOBEC3A.

Human cells can detect and destroy uracil bases in DNA, and only by inhibiting this ability were Richardson et al. able to observe APOBEC3A mutations in new LINE-1 copies within the genomes of living cells.
Richardson et al. speculate that the activity of APOBEC3 enzymes must balance limiting the spread of retrotransposons and minimizing the mutation of the cell's own DNA.
APOBEC3 enzymes can cause mutations in cancers and have been proposed as new targets for anti-cancer drugs.
Normal wear and tear, exposure to chemicals, and ultraviolet light can all damage DNA.
Cells rely on a range of sensors and mechanisms to detect and repair damaged DNA.
Cells package DNA molecules inside structures called histones to protect them against damage.
Double-strand breaks are one of the most serious forms of DNA damage.
Double-strand breaks are detected by an enzyme called ATM (ataxia-telangiectasia mutated).
Double-strand breaks can be repaired in two ways.
Bringing the broken DNA strands back together is an obvious method to repair double-strand breaks, but this method is error prone.
Using templates to generate new DNA to repair double-strand breaks is less prone to error, but it can only happen at certain times of the cell cycle.
Some cancers are linked to the faulty repair of double-strand breaks.
A type of kidney cancer called clear cell renal carcinoma is linked to a lack of activity by a protein called p53, even in individuals who do not have mutations in the gene for p53.
Many people with clear cell renal carcinoma have mutations in the gene for a protein called SETD2.
SETD2 must be present for DNA repair to take place because SETD2 modifies the histones so that they can recruit the enzymes that repair the DNA via the template approach.
The template approach to DNA repair is relatively error free.
SETD2 may be particularly important for repairing damage to genes without introducing errors.
Mutations in SETD2 are sufficient to inactivate p53.
The gene for p53 impedes the proliferation of cells with genomic aberrations, such as double-strand breaks.
The gene for p53 is mutated in most cancers.
The muscles that allow animals to move are built predominantly of cells called myofibers.
Myofibers develop via a regulated set of events called differentiation.
In adults, muscle regeneration after an injury occurs when new myofibers differentiate from satellite cells that already reside within the muscles.
Differentiation is regulated at the genetic level, and the development of myofibers relies on the activation of muscle-specific genes.
A gene’s expression is typically controlled via a nearby regulatory region of DNA called a promoter that can be recognized by various molecular machines made from protein complexes.
In most adult tissues, regulatory machineries contain a complex called TFIID.

Previously it was reported that the TFIID complex was eliminated from cells during muscle differentiation and that an alternative protein complex called TBP2/TAF3 recognizes and regulates the promoters of muscle-specific genes.
Malecova et al. have discovered that TFIID is present, albeit at reduced amounts, in differentiated muscles and that TFIID drives the activation of muscle-specific genes during differentiation.
Experiments showed that the TBP2 protein is not required for differentiation of muscle cells or for the regeneration of injured muscles and is absent in muscle cells.
DNA in a cell is under constant stress from environmental factors, such as ultraviolet light, or from damage caused by the replication process.
Environmental factors and damage caused by the replication process can cause breaks in the genome, which if left unrepaired can lead to cancer or cell death.

One of the most accurate ways to repair a broken fragment of DNA is through recombination, whereby an undamaged copy of the sequence is located in another DNA molecule and used as a template to replace the missing fragment.
DNA recombination is regulated by more than a dozen proteins that help recruit the enzyme RAD51 to sites of DNA damage and trigger RAD51's search for complementary sequences of DNA.
A molecule known as PALB2 binds to DNA repair proteins and coordinates their activity.
If PALB2 or the other DNA repair proteins become mutated, this can increase the risk of cancerous growths in various tissues, including the breasts and ovaries.
PALB2 interacts directly with DNA, and this interaction is an important part of the DNA repair process.
Even in the absence of RAD51, PALB2 is still able to recombine short fragments of DNA sequence.
PALB2 initiates recombination using single strands of DNA or a DNA-like molecule known as RNA (ribonucleic acid).
The ability of PALB2 to initiate recombination using RNA may be particularly important if the molecular machines needed to replicate DNA and synthesize RNA collide on the same DNA molecule.
The new role of PALB2 in DNA recombination could lead to the discovery of other DNA repair mechanisms and could be used to predict which PALB2 mutations are more likely to cause cancer.
Patients who are at greater risk of cancer due to PALB2 mutations could be treated with more advanced therapies to increase their chances of recovery.

The colour patterns that mark an animal's skin, hair, or feathers—called the pigmentation pattern—can be very important for the animal's survival and fitness by helping the animal to hide from predators or to attract a mate.
Adult zebrafish have a characteristic pigmentation pattern of horizontal dark and light stripes on their bodies and fins.
There are three types of pigment cell that create the pigmentation pattern in adult zebrafish.
Xanthophores and iridophores are found all over the body of adult zebrafish.
The dark stripes on adult zebrafish contain melanophore cells.
The silvery, reflective iridophores are the first pigment cells to populate the skin of adult zebrafish, giving rise to the first light stripe.
Iridophores form a dense network of cells that breaks up to form the darker stripes on adult zebrafish.
Iridophores are not required to form stripes in the fins of adult zebrafish, suggesting that patterning occurs differently in the fins and the body.
Mutations to a gene called leopard, or leo for short, cause spots to form on the skin of the zebrafish in place of the usual stripes.
The leopard (leo) gene encodes a member of the connexin family of proteins, which form channels in the membranes that surround cells.
The channels formed by connexin proteins—known as gap junctions—allow neighbouring cells to communicate with each other.
Each gap junction is made up of two half channels, with one half coming from each neighbouring cell.
If the two half channels of a gap junction are identical, the gap junction is known as homomeric.
Heteromeric gap junctions are made from two different half channels, each consisting of a different connexin protein.
The connexin encoded by the leopard (leo) gene is required for both homomeric and heteromeric gap junctions to form between melanophores and xanthophores.
Irion et al. discovered a new mutation to the leopard (leo) gene that completely disrupts the patterning of the zebrafish.

A technique called a genetic screen revealed that the same patterning defects are also seen in the body of zebrafish with mutations to another gene called luchs, which encodes a different connexin protein than the one produced by leopard (leo).
The fins of zebrafish with mutant versions of the luchs gene remain striped.

Heteromeric gap junctions formed from the connexins produced by leopard (leo) and luchs are important for xanthophores and melanophores to communicate with each other and form the stripy patterning seen on the body of the zebrafish.
The signals transmitted through the gap junctions may make the iridophores adopt the looser arrangement that is required for the dark stripes to form on the zebrafish body.

Species in the crucifer family, which includes mustard, cabbages, and the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana, can defend themselves with camalexin, a compound produced soon after the plant receives signals from its attacker.
The DNA sequences of genes that control the production of camalexin need to be physically accessible to the cell for these genes to be read, interpreted, and ultimately converted into proteins.
The availability of DNA sequences for gene expression is controlled, in part, by adding or removing chemical groups onto histones, the spool-like structures which DNA wraps around.
Precisely controlled chemical modifications on histones help to activate or repress a gene.
Activating and inhibiting chemical groups can be present in the same location on histones, creating what is known as a bivalent chromatin domain.
Zhao et al. investigated whether histone modifications regulate when Arabidopsis thaliana produces camalexin in response to an attack.

A combination of bioinformatics and experimental approaches highlighted two chemical modifications, one repressive and the other activating, which were present on the same histone, forming a previously unknown bivalent chromatin domain.
Mutant Arabidopsis thaliana plants which did not carry the two histone modifications could not produce camalexin at the right time.
Under normal conditions, both histone modifications were present on the same histone in Arabidopsis thaliana.
When Arabidopsis thaliana was under attack, the level of the repressive histone modification decreased and the level of the activating histone modification increased, leading to gene activation.
Both histone modifications are required for camalexin genes in Arabidopsis thaliana to respond appropriately to signals from a harmful agent.
Sperm cells have tails called flagella that propel sperm cells towards an egg.
Other cells have similar, but shorter, structures called cilia that sway back and forth on the surface of those cells.
Cilia sweep dust and debris out of human lungs and airways.
Cilia have a number of other crucial roles during development.
Faulty cilia can lead to serious birth defects, as well as diseases of the kidneys and respiratory system.
Cilia and flagella are made from proteins that are assembled in a process called intraflagellar transport or IFT.
Around 20 proteins are thought to be involved in the intraflagellar transport process, but the precise role of many of these proteins remains unclear.

Ishikawa et al. compared the versions of one of the intraflagellar transport proteins, called TTC26, that are found in zebrafish, mouse cells, and a single-celled alga called Chlamydomonas reinhardtii that uses a pair of flagella to move around.
The TTC26 protein localizes to the cilia of mouse cells and can be seen to move along these cilia in a manner typical of other intraflagellar transport proteins.
Blocking production of TTC26 in zebrafish embryos caused these embryos to fail to develop the correct left–right asymmetry.
Zebrafish embryos with blocked production of TTC26 had problems with their eyes, ears, and kidneys.
Although cilia were present in the affected zebrafish embryos with blocked TTC26 production, these cilia were shortened and moved abnormally.
Algae that had a mutation in the gene that codes for TTC26 had short cilia that moved in an abnormal way.
The findings of Ishikawa et al. suggest that TTC26 may help to transport a specific subset of proteins into the cilia.

If other intraflagellar transport proteins are also shown to carry distinct subsets of cargo, this might explain why as many as 20 different proteins are involved in the intraflagellar transport process.
Lysosomes are specialized, enclosed compartments within cells with harsh chemical conditions where enzymes break down large molecules into smaller component parts.
The products of the enzymatic reactions in lysosomes are transported out of the lysosome by transporter proteins so that the cell can use them to build new molecules.
Only a few lysosomal transporters have been thoroughly studied despite their importance.
A protein called MFSD1 had previously been identified as a potential lysosomal transporter, but its precise role had not been described.
Massa López et al. genetically modified mice so that the mice could no longer make the MFSD1 transporter.
Mice that could no longer make the MFSD1 transporter developed severe liver damage.
A specific type of cell important for lining blood vessels in the liver seemed to be lost in the MFSD1 deficient mice.
Older MFSD1 deficient mice had more tumors in their livers compared to normal mice.
Massa López et al. found that MFSD1 deficient mice had strikingly low levels of a protein called GLMP.
Another strain of genetically modified mice missing GLMP was analyzed to better understand the relationship between GLMP and MFSD1.
Mice without GLMP were found to have very similar liver problems to those observed in the mice lacking MFSD1.
GLMP deficient mice had low levels of the MFSD1 protein.
MFSD1 and GLMP physically interact with each other, and GLMP seems to protect MFSD1 from being degraded in the harsh internal environment of the lysosome.
Both GLMP and MFSD1 are needed to form a stable lysosomal transporter.
Characterizing MFSD1 is important for scientists attempting to understand how the lysosomal membrane and transporters work.
The findings about MFSD1 and GLMP may shed light on how defects in lysosomal transporters contribute to metabolic disease.
Before a cell divides, the cell must first copy all of its genetic material.
Any mistakes that are made during the copying of genetic material are called mutations.
Mutations can give rise to new traits but are mostly harmful to the cells or cause cancer.
Cells have evolved tools that can efficiently spot mutations and repair them.
One of the main tools that cells use to repair mutations is called mismatch repair (MMR).
Defects in the cell's mismatch repair tools can allow many mutations to accumulate and cause severe problems.
Zhao et al. looked at the genomes of tumors where mismatch repair was not working properly to see what makes these ‘MMR-deficient tumors’ different from other tumors.
MMR-deficient tumors have similar patterns of mutations to those seen in egg and sperm cells.

The similarity of mutation patterns in MMR-deficient tumors to those in egg and sperm cells suggests that mutations not corrected by mismatch repair are an important source of genetic differences between different humans and between humans and their ancestors.
Identifying cancerous tumors that are MMR-deficient is vital because these tumors tend not to respond to commonly used cancer treatments.
Current clinical methods to identify MMR-deficient tumors often fail or produce results that are difficult to interpret.
MMR-deficient tumors commonly contain mutations called indels, where short fragments of DNA are inserted or deleted into longer DNA sequences.
Zhao et al. have found 59 indels that can be used to detect MMR-deficient tumors, where each indel had been identified in several tumors taken from different tissues.
The new approach using 59 indels allowed MMR-deficiency to be identified in several types of tumor, including colon and ovarian cancers, with greater sensitivity and accuracy than existing methods.
The indels in MMR-deficient tumors reduce the ability of the tumors to repair a type of DNA damage called double-strand breaks.
Double-strand breaks are DNA damage in which both strands of DNA that make up the double helix are broken and the DNA chain is severed.
Double-strand breaks are very harmful to a cell.
Making more double-strand breaks could form part of a more effective treatment against MMR-deficient tumors.
In many animals, the skull is made of several separate bones that are loosely joined during childhood and only fuse into one piece when the animal stops growing.
Carpenter syndrome is a genetic disease that causes the bones of the skull to fuse early in life, stopping the skull from growing correctly.
Carpenter syndrome is often caused by changes to the gene responsible for making a protein called RAB23.
RAB23 helps move other molecules and cell components between different parts of the cell and is therefore involved in a number of cellular processes.
Previous studies suggest that RAB23 has a role in many parts of the body during development.
It is unclear which cells in the skull depend on RAB23 activity and how the RAB23 protein is controlled.
Hasan et al. grew pieces of developing skull bones taken from mice lacking the RAB23 protein in the laboratory to study RAB23 function.
Examining samples of developing skull bones from mice lacking RAB23 revealed that RAB23 is active in osteoblasts, which add new bone to the edge of each piece of the skull as it grows.
RAB23 regulates two cellular signaling pathways called the hedgehog pathway and the fibroblast growth factor pathway that interact with one another and coordinate skull development.
RAB23 controls the growth and fusion of skull bones in developing animals.
Most cells in the bodies of humans and other animals carry the same DNA, which is arranged into sections known as genes.
The marked differences between cell types arise because different sets of genes are switched on or ‘expressed’.
Proteins called transcription factors control which genes are expressed by binding to DNA and recruiting groups of accessory proteins.
It is thought that some accessory proteins may provide energy for the process of gene expression, but it is unknown whether the energy is used continuously or only for a short time.
Insights from physics suggest that continuous use of energy during gene expression could have more powerful effects than short-term energy use.
In 2014, a team of researchers reported using a microscopy approach, known as single-molecule imaging, to follow two transcription factors called Sox2 and Oct4 in cells from mice.
The 2014 researchers concluded that Sox2 and Oct4 had a specific order of binding to DNA, with Sox2 often binding first and then assisting Oct4 to bind.
Biddle et al. report that the claim made in the 2014 study about the order of binding of Sox2 and Oct4 is unsupported because of errors in the way the data were analyzed.
Biddle et al. argue that the 2014 study actually calculated a measure of whether energy is being continuously used when Sox2 and Oct4 bind to DNA, not an order of binding.
Biddle et al. reanalyzed the data from the 2014 work and concluded that Sox2 increases the extent of Oct4 binding to DNA, while Oct4 decreases the amount of Sox2 binding to DNA.
Mathematical models suggest that the continuous use of energy may explain how Sox2 and Oct4 bind to DNA.
Alternatively, Sox2 and Oct4 may help each other to bind at some sites on DNA and hinder each other from binding in other places, even if energy is only used for a short time.
These findings reveal that there is unexpected complexity in how transcription factors bind to DNA.
Including physics in the analysis may help describe more accurately the biology of how transcription factors determine gene expression.

Understanding how transcription factors determine gene expression will shed new light on many important biological questions and may aid the development of gene therapy and other new medical techniques.
The lateral prefrontal cortex has a critical role in many of the processes seen as hallmarks of human cognition, such as reasoning, planning, and problem-solving.
Individuals with damage to the lateral prefrontal cortex are disorganized and easily distracted, and may show behaviors that are inappropriate for their context.
The involvement of the lateral prefrontal cortex in a wide range of processes makes the lateral prefrontal cortex difficult to study.
Brain imaging revealed that the rear (posterior) part of the lateral prefrontal cortex processes an individual’s current situation.
Brain imaging revealed that the front (anterior) part of the lateral prefrontal cortex prepares for future situations.
Areas in the middle of the lateral prefrontal cortex process both current and future types of information.
The central areas of the lateral prefrontal cortex have stronger connections to the anterior and posterior regions than the anterior and posterior regions have to the central areas.
In cognitively demanding situations, the middle areas of the lateral prefrontal cortex receive input from both anterior regions and posterior regions.

The middle areas of the lateral prefrontal cortex combine information about current needs from posterior regions and future needs from anterior regions to select behaviors that take into account both present circumstances and longer-term goals.
The middle areas of the lateral prefrontal cortex are well positioned to play the part of the brain’s chief executive by providing a strategic overview.
The lateral prefrontal cortex shows abnormal activity in disorders such as schizophrenia.
Inflammation is an immune response that helps the body to repair damaged tissues and defend itself against bacteria and other harmful microbes.
Immune cells called macrophages stimulate inflammation when they detect bacteria and other microbes.
The strength of the inflammatory response is tightly controlled to prevent too much inflammation when it is not necessary.
An inability to control the activity of macrophages can lead to excessive inflammation that can in itself cause injury.
Inflammatory bowel diseases, including Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, occur when the intestine becomes inflamed in response to the bacteria that normally live there.
Most patients with inflammatory bowel diseases first present symptoms as young adults, but in rare cases the symptoms appear during infancy.
Some patients who develop symptoms early in life carry a mutation in a gene encoding IL10R, a receptor protein that normally inhibits the ability of macrophages to cause inflammation.
It was not known exactly when the inflammation begins in infants.
Mice are often used in research as models of human health and disease.
Redhu et al. investigated the role of IL10R in the intestines of infant mice.
The intestines of mutant mice that lacked the IL10R protein became inflamed as they were weaned from breast milk to a solid diet.
The inflammation in the intestines of mutant mice was accompanied by a greater increase in the number of actively recruited macrophages compared to normal mice.
Macrophages in the mutant mice activate many genes involved in inflammation.
The transition from breast milk to a solid diet is accompanied by large increases in intestinal bacteria.
Treating the mice with antibiotics decreased the number of bacteria in the intestines and reduced the level of inflammation.
Treating the mice with a compound that killed macrophages reduced the level of inflammation in the intestines.
IL10R prevents macrophages from causing inflammation when infant mice are weaned.
Treatments that modify intestinal macrophages, as well as bacteria, could help infants that have, or are at risk of developing inflammatory bowel disease.
These findings might aid the development of new treatments for older patients with inflammatory bowel diseases in the longer term.
Before an animal is born, a protein called bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) plays a key role in establishing the difference between the front and the back of the animal.
Cells nearer the front of the embryo contain higher amounts of the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP), whilst cells nearer the back have progressively lower levels of BMP.
The gradient of bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) concentration affects the identity of the cells, with the level of BMP in each cell dictating what parts of the body are made where.

The prevailing view among scientists is that the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) gradient is created by an opposing gradient of another protein called Chordin, which is found at high levels at the back of the embryo and lower levels near the front.
Chordin inhibits bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) and the interaction between the two proteins establishes the gradients that create order across the embryo.
Zinski et al. used computer models to investigate how the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) gradient is created.

Comparing the computer models to precise experimental measurements of bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) activity in zebrafish embryos suggested that a source-sink model, rather than the opposing Chordin gradient, may be responsible for the pattern of BMP found in the embryo.
In the source-sink model, bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) is produced at the front of the embryo and moves towards the back end by diffusion.
At the back of the embryo, bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) is mopped up by Chordin, resulting in a constant gradient of BMP along the embryo.
Many other processes that control how animals grow and develop rely on the formation of similar protein gradients.
Understanding how animals grow and develop may help researchers to develop strategies to regrow tissues and organs in human patients.
When groups of people are separated for generations, the DNA sequence in the two groups’ genomes will change in different ways.
Looking at the differences in the genomes of people from the same population can help researchers to understand and reconstruct the historical interactions that brought their ancestors together.
The mixing of two populations that were previously separate is known as admixture.
Africa as a continent has few written records of its history.
It is somewhat unknown which important movements of people in the past generated the populations found in modern-day Africa.
Busby et al. have attempted to use DNA to reconstruct the last 4000 years of genetic history in African populations.
The new analysis showed that all African populations are the result of historical admixture events.
Busby et al. could characterize these historical admixture events to an unprecedented level of detail.
Multiple ethnic groups from The Gambia and Mali all show signs of sharing the same set of ancestors from West Africa, Europe, and Asia who mixed around 2000 years ago.
Evidence of a migration of people from Central West Africa, known as the Bantu expansion, was detected and was shown to carry genes to the south and east.
Human DNA contains more than three billion nucleotides.
Each nucleotide in human DNA can be adenine, cytosine, guanine, or thymine.
Groups of three neighboring nucleotides within human DNA are used to represent the 20 amino acids that are used to make proteins.
Changing one nucleotide in DNA can cause one amino acid to be replaced by a different amino acid in the protein encoded by that stretch of DNA.
The codons AAA and AAG code for the amino acid lysine in human DNA.
The codons AAC and AAT code for the amino acid asparagine in human DNA.
Missense gene variants are changes in DNA that replace one amino acid with a different amino acid and can also increase or decrease the expression of the gene.
Every person has thousands of missense gene variants, including about 12,000 inherited from their parents.
Missense gene variants sometimes have no consequence but can be harmful if replacing the correct amino acid prevents the protein from performing an important task.
Missense gene variants in genes that encode immune system proteins are likely to play a role in diseases of the immune system.
Variants near a gene called Rasgrp1 have been linked to two autoimmune diseases, type 1 diabetes and Graves’ disease, in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the body’s own cells and tissues.
Mice with a missense gene variant in Rasgrp1 show signs of autoimmune disease.
T cells, which are white blood cells that have a central role in the immune system, develop normally in mice with the Rasgrp1 missense gene variant despite the mutation.
T helper cells accumulate in large numbers in mice with the Rasgrp1 missense gene variant and stimulate B cells to produce autoantibodies.
The production of autoantibodies is a common feature of autoimmune diseases.

The origins of the T helper cells in mice with the Rasgrp1 missense gene variant were traced to excessive activity on a signaling pathway that involves a protein called mTOR (mechanistic target of rapamycin).
Treatment with the drug rapamycin counteracted the accumulation of T helper cells and reduced the level of autoimmune activity in mice with the Rasgrp1 missense gene variant.
Neurons that arise in the adult nervous system originate from neural stem cells and neural progenitor cells.
Neural stem cells have long lives, much of which they spend in a quiescent state.
Neural stem cells can give rise to neural progenitor cells, which proliferate rapidly during their short lives and then differentiate into neurons or glia.
It has not been possible to identify or purify neural stem cells directly from the tissue.
Neural stem and progenitor cells have usually been studied retrospectively based on their ability to form colonies in laboratory cell cultures.

A region of the brain called the subventricular zone contains both neural stem cells and neural progenitor cells and is one of only two regions of the brain where neural stem cells are found in adult mammals.
When cells from the subventricular zone are cultured in a way that allows the cells to freely float around rather than growing on a surface, a few percent form spherical colonies called neurospheres.
Neurosphere-forming cells can self-renew and differentiate into neurons and glia.
The ability of cells to form neurospheres has generally been taken as evidence that the cells are stem cells.
The exact relationship between neural stem cells and neurosphere-forming cells has been uncertain.
Mich, Signer et al. have used a technique called flow cytometry to identify and isolate neural stem cells and neurosphere-forming cells directly from the subventricular zone.

The neural stem cells, which Mich, Signer et al. term pre-GEPCOT cells based on an acronym of the markers used to isolate the cells, were long-lived and quiescent but lacked the ability to form colonies in culture.
The neurosphere-forming cells, named GEPCOT cells, were short-lived and highly proliferative in the brain.
The cells that form neurospheres in culture are not stem cells, and real stem cells are not able to form colonies under existing culture conditions.

The identification of undifferentiated pre-GEPCOT and GEPCOT cells will make it possible to directly study the properties of these cells inside the mouse brain and to isolate live cells to test how they function.
Current tests using neurospheres do not detect neural stem cells as commonly assumed, highlighting the need for new tests to study neural stem cell function.
Xie, Pu, Metzger et al. developed an experimental approach that can evolve reconstructed ancestral proteins that existed deep in the past.

Using the experimental approach developed by Xie, Pu, Metzger et al., it is possible to replay evolution multiple times from various historical starting points under conditions similar to those that existed long ago.
Xie, Pu, Metzger et al. studied proteins belonging to the BCL-2 family, which originated some 800 million years ago.
BCL-2 family proteins have diversified greatly over time in both their genetic sequences and their ability to bind to specific partner proteins called co-regulators.
Xie, Pu, Metzger et al. synthesized BCL-2 proteins that existed at various times in the past.

Each ancestral BCL-2 protein synthesized by Xie, Pu, Metzger et al. was allowed to evolve repeatedly under natural selection to acquire the same co-regulator binding functions that evolved during history.
At the end of each evolutionary trajectory, the genetic sequence of the resulting BCL-2 proteins was recorded.

The outcomes of evolution were almost completely unpredictable because trajectories initiated from the same ancestral protein produced proteins with very different sequences, and proteins launched from different ancestral starting points were even more dissimilar.
Further experiments identified the mutations in each evolutionary trajectory that caused changes in co-regulator binding.
When the mutations identified in each evolutionary trajectory were introduced into other ancestral proteins, they did not yield the same change in function.
Early chance events influenced each BCL-2 protein’s evolution in an unpredictable way by opening and closing the evolutionary paths available to the protein in the future.
The results suggest that BCL-2 proteins, in all their various forms, are unique products of a particular, unpredictable course of history set in motion by ancient chance events.
A group of flexible filamentous viruses can cause serious diseases in a wide variety of crops and other plants.
Each virus particle of flexible filamentous viruses contains a single molecule called ribonucleic acid (RNA), which is protected by hundreds of copies of a coat protein.
The ribonucleic acid (RNA) and coat proteins in flexible filamentous viruses are arranged in a helical fashion to make a flexible rod-shaped particle.
The flexibility of flexible filamentous viruses makes it difficult to carry out in-depth studies of their three-dimensional structures.
The interactions between the ribonucleic acid (RNA) and coat proteins that form the structure of each flexible filamentous virus particle are currently unknown.
Agirrezabala et al. used a technique called cryo-electron microscopy (cryoEM) to generate a highly detailed three-dimensional model of a flexible filamentous virus called Pepino Mosaic Virus.
Agirrezabala et al.'s findings reveal how Pepino Mosaic Virus particles assemble and the interactions between the coat protein and the single-stranded ribonucleic acid (ssRNA).
The structure of the coat protein from Pepino Mosaic Virus is very similar to the structure of nucleoproteins from a group of viruses called the Phleboviruses, which infect animals.

The similarity between the coat protein of Pepino Mosaic Virus and the nucleoproteins of Phleboviruses suggests that the gene encoding these proteins has been transferred between the two groups of viruses during evolution.
Bacteria can cause diseases, but bacteriophages are viruses that prey on bacteria.
The T7 bacteriophage preys on various strains of Escherichia coli, a type of bacteria often found in the human gut.
Many Escherichia coli strains are inoffensive or even beneficial to human health, but some Escherichia coli strains can be deadly.
Bacteriophages identify and interact with their specific bacterial targets through a structure known as the receptor binding protein, or RBP.
It is still unclear exactly how the receptor binding protein helps bacteriophages recognize which type of bacteria to infect.
Huss et al. mapped out and modified the receptor binding protein structure in T7 bacteriophage to make the virus more efficient and specific about which strain of Escherichia coli it kills.
The role of each building block in the tip of the receptor binding protein was meticulously dissected in this study.

The dissection of the receptor binding protein generated the knowledge required to genetically engineer a large number of different T7 bacteriophages, each with a slight variation in their receptor binding protein.
The genetically engineered T7 bacteriophages with variations in their receptor binding protein were exposed to various strains of bacteria.

Monitoring the bacteriophages that survived and multiplied the most after infecting different strains of Escherichia coli revealed which receptor binding protein building blocks are important for efficiency and specificity.

Engineering highly active T7 bacteriophage variants against an Escherichia coli strain that causes urinary tract infections confirmed the importance of receptor binding protein building blocks for efficiency and specificity.
Small changes to bacteriophages can make a big difference to their ability to infect their bacterial prey.
The approaches developed by Huss et al. help to understand exactly how the receptor binding protein allows a virus to infect a specific type of bacteria.

Understanding how the receptor binding protein allows bacteriophages to infect specific bacteria could one day pave the way for new therapies that harness those viruses to fight increasingly resistant bacterial infections.
The inside of a cell contains many different compartments called organelles, which are separated by membranes.
Each organelle is composed of a unique set of proteins and performs specific roles in the cell.
The endoplasmic reticulum, or ER for short, is an organelle where many proteins are produced.
Most of the proteins produced in the endoplasmic reticulum are then released from the cell or sorted to other organelles.
The endoplasmic reticulum has a strict quality control system that ensures any faulty proteins are quickly marked for the cell to destroy.
The destruction process of faulty proteins does not happen in the endoplasmic reticulum, so faulty proteins first need to leave this organelle.
The extraction of faulty proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum is achieved by a group of proteins known as endoplasmic reticulum-associated protein degradation machinery, or ERAD for short.
To extract a faulty protein from the endoplasmic reticulum, proteins of the ER and outside the ER cooperate.
An ERAD protein called Doa10 attaches a small protein tag called ubiquitin to the faulty proteins to mark them for destruction.
Outside of the endoplasmic reticulum, a protein called Cdc48 grabs the ubiquitin tag and pulls.
Many of the proteins made by the endoplasmic reticulum have tethers that anchor them firmly to the membrane, making them much harder to remove.
Schmidt et al. rebuilt the ERAD machinery in a test tube by purifying proteins from yeast and inserting them into artificial membranes, allowing closer study of each part of the process.
Attaching ubiquitin tags to faulty proteins is only one part of Doa10's role; Doa10 also participates in the extraction of faulty proteins from the membrane.
Part of Doa10 resides within the membrane, and this membrane-spanning domain can interact with faulty proteins, loosening their membrane anchors.
The pulling force exerted by Cdc48 from outside the membrane causes the faulty proteins to unfold, allowing them to pass through the membrane.
A build-up of faulty proteins can cause diseases like neurodegeneration.
Humans and other animals reflect on past experiences of similar situations to choose the best option when faced with a decision to make.

In an uncertain situation, the decision process requires balancing two competing priorities: exploiting options that are expected to be rewarding and exploring alternatives that could be more valuable.
Decision making and exploration are disrupted in many mental disorders, some of which can differ in either presentation or risk of development across women and men.
Chen et al. studied exploration in male and female mice as the mice played a video game.
The mice had the option to touch one of two locations on a screen for a chance to win a small reward.
The likelihood of success was different between the two options, and the mice were incentivized to determine which was the more rewarding button.

While the mice were similarly successful in finding rewards regardless of sex, on average male mice were more likely to keep exploring between the options while female mice more quickly gained confidence in an option.
The differences in exploration and exploitation between male and female mice were stronger during uncertain periods of learning and exploration than when making choices in a well-known situation.
There was as much variability within a sex as was seen between sexes in the exploration and exploitation behaviors of male and female mice.
Sex mechanisms, along with many other influences, cause individual differences in the cognitive processes important for decision making.

The approach used by Chen et al. could help to study individual differences in cognition in other species and shed light on how individual differences in decision-making processes could contribute to risk and resilience to mental disorders.
Animals and other multicellular organisms all have at least some ability to regenerate lost or wounded tissues.
Zebrafish are particularly good at regenerating lost or damaged body parts to the extent that they can replace them with exact replicas of the originals.
In 2015, a team of researchers found that some mutant zebrafish that lack blood cells including immune cells are unable to regenerate lost tissues.
The cells that are primed to regenerate die in mutant zebrafish that lack blood cells including immune cells.
Many immune cells have roles in fighting infection and in responding to tissue damage.
When a tissue is damaged, the area often becomes inflamed as white blood cells called macrophages flock to the damaged area to protect it from infection and remove damaged cells.
Hasegawa et al. used genetic approaches to investigate the role of inflammation in tissue regeneration in zebrafish.
Several genes involved in inflammation, including one called interleukin 1b, were active over longer periods of time in mutant zebrafish compared with normal zebrafish.
The gene interleukin 1b produces a signal protein and this prolonged activity causes the primed regenerative cells to die in mutant zebrafish.
The primed regenerative cells can survive if interleukin 1b activity is quickly suppressed by macrophages.
In order for tissues to regenerate properly in zebrafish, interleukin 1b needs to be active for only a short period of time.
Some inflammation is needed for tissues to regenerate, but a more severe inflammatory response can block the process in zebrafish.
Anti-inflammatory signals produced by macrophages may have the potential to be used as drugs to cure chronic inflammatory diseases and boost tissue regeneration potential in humans.
